# Ecommerce Marketing Agency Cost: Pricing Models and Real Value
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/how-much-does-a-dtc-agency-cost
Summary: Ecommerce marketing agency cost explained: retainer, % of ad spend, performance and hybrid fees, hidden costs, and how to judge value with margin and MER.

Direct Answer: Ecommerce marketing agency cost depends on the pricing model and the scope of work. Most agencies charge a monthly retainer, a percentage of ad spend, a performance fee or a hybrid. The useful comparison is total cost, including creative and tools, against the extra contribution margin the agency produces for your brand.

      
      Total agency cost: Everything you pay to have an agency run growth: the management fee, creative production, software and any performance bonus. Ad spend goes to the platforms and is normally billed separately.

      
        
## Why ecommerce marketing agency cost varies so much

        Ask five agencies for a quote and you will get five structures that are hard to compare. [Ecommerce marketing agency](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/) cost is not one number, because agencies sell different things under the same label. One runs your Meta account and nothing else. Another writes creative, edits [UGC](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/viral-creatives), rebuilds your product page and runs [Klaviyo flows](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/klaviyo-email-sms-agency). A third mostly reports on what the platforms already do automatically.
So before you compare fees, compare scope. Write down which channels the agency will manage, how many new ads it will ship each month, who produces the footage, whether store and conversion work is included, and who owns tracking. Two quotes that look far apart can be close once you price in the work one of them leaves for you.
The other reason costs vary is risk. An agency paid only on results carries more risk, so it prices that in, chooses clients carefully, or both. A flat retainer moves the risk to you. Neither is better by default. The right structure is the one that rewards the agency for the outcome you actually care about, which for most DTC brands is profitable new customer growth.

        
        
        
      
        
## The five agency pricing models

        Almost every DTC agency uses one of these models or a mix of them. Each one creates a different incentive, and that incentive matters more than the headline fee.

        
        ModelHow it worksWorks best whenWatch out forMonthly retainerFixed fee for a defined scopeScope is clear and spend is stablePaying the same in slow months; scope creepPercentage of ad spendFee rises and falls with spendSpend is growing and the agency drives creativeIncentive to raise spend rather than profitPerformance feeShare of revenue or profit above a baselineTracking is clean and the baseline is agreedDisputes over attribution and baselineHybridLower base fee plus a percentage or bonusYou want shared risk with predictable costComplex terms that are hard to auditProject feeOne-off price for a build, audit or launchYou need a store build, setup or Q4 pushNo ongoing ownership once the project ends
        
      
        
## Example arithmetic: one brand, four fee structures

        The figures below are an illustration we made up to show how the models behave. They are not market rates and not our prices. Assume a brand spends $40,000 a month on ads and does $150,000 in revenue, of which $30,000 is above an agreed baseline.
Notice what happens when spend doubles. The retainer stays flat, the percentage fee doubles, and the performance fee only grows if revenue above the baseline grows. That is why the percentage model needs a profit guardrail, such as a minimum [MER](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/mer) the agency must hold before it raises budgets.

        
        Example structureFee at $40K spendFee if spend doubles to $80KRetainer of $5,000 a month$5,000$5,00010% of ad spend$4,000$8,00010% of revenue above baseline ($30,000)$3,000Depends on new revenue above baseline$2,500 base plus 5% of ad spend$4,500$6,500
        
      
        
## What drives the cost up or down

        Agency pricing tracks the hours and skill a brand needs each month. These five factors move it most.

        - Spend level: more spend means more campaigns, more testing and more risk to manage, so fees usually rise with budget even under a retainer.
- Creative volume: an agency shipping 30 to 50 new ads a month needs strategists, editors and creators. Volume is the most expensive part of the work and usually the most valuable.
- Number of channels: Meta alone is cheaper to run than Meta plus TikTok, [Google Shopping](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/google-shopping-ads-agency) and Performance Max, because each channel needs its own testing and reporting.
- CRO and store work: product page rebuilds, bundles, post-purchase upsells and speed work add design and development hours.
- Tracking and data: setting up [Conversions API](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/conversions-api), fixing attribution and building reporting is front-loaded work that often appears as an onboarding fee.

        
        
      
        
## Hidden costs founders miss

        The management fee is rarely the full bill. Budget for these before you sign, and ask the agency which ones are included.

        - Creative production: UGC creator fees, product samples, shipping to creators, editing and usage rights. If the agency only manages ads, you will pay for footage separately.
- Software: attribution tools, analytics, creative testing tools, Shopify apps for bundles or reviews, and email platform costs that rise with list size.
- Testing budget: new concepts need spend before they prove themselves. That spend is real money even when a test loses.
- Onboarding and audits: some agencies charge a setup fee for tracking, account restructuring and strategy.
- Contract terms: minimum terms and long notice periods are a cost if the fit is wrong.
- Your team time: approvals, product briefings and weekly calls still need someone on your side.

        
        
      
        
## How to judge value with contribution margin and MER

        The right question is not whether a fee is high but whether the agency adds more [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin) than it costs. Contribution margin here means revenue minus product cost, shipping, payment fees, ad spend and marketing costs.
Example only: before the agency, a brand does $120,000 a month on $40,000 of ad spend, an MER of 3.0. Its gross margin after product, shipping and fees is 60%, so contribution is $120,000 x 0.6 = $72,000, minus $40,000 spend, which leaves $32,000.
Three months later it does $160,000 on $45,000 spend, an MER of about 3.56. Contribution is $160,000 x 0.6 = $96,000, minus $45,000 spend, a $5,000 fee and $3,000 of creative, which leaves $43,000. The agency costs $8,000 and adds $11,000 a month, so it pays for itself with room to spare.
Run the same test on any quote. Use MER, total revenue divided by total marketing spend, rather than platform ROAS, because platform numbers can rise while the business stands still.

        
        
        
      
        
## Questions to ask before you sign

        These questions expose most mismatches before money changes hands.

        - Exactly what is included each month, and what is billed as extra?
- How many new creatives will you ship monthly, and who films them?
- Which metric do you report on: platform ROAS, MER or contribution margin?
- What happens to the fee if spend goes up or down?
- Who owns the ad account, pixel, creative files and data if we part ways?
- What is the minimum term and notice period?
- Who works on my account day to day, and how many accounts do they run?
- Can I see real [case studies](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies) from brands at my revenue level?

        
        
      
        
## How Brand Scaling prices an engagement

        We do not publish a price list, because the right structure depends on your channels, creative needs and unit economics. Every engagement starts with a [Brand Growth Audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/book), a one-on-one review of your ad account, creative, store and margins with Gaurav. After the audit we quote a monthly retainer, a percentage of ad spend, a performance component or a mix, whichever matches the work.
Our partners are usually DTC brands with product-market fit doing roughly $20K to $2M+ a month, spending at least $10K to $20K a month on paid ads. Below that level, a full agency fee is often a large share of the budget, and a focused audit or project can be the better first step.
Whoever you talk to, ask for the quote in writing with the scope attached: channels, creative volume, reporting cadence and who owns which task. That single page makes it far easier to compare agencies fairly and to hold the one you choose to what was promised.

        
        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is a percentage of ad spend a fair way to pay an agency?
It can be, if there is a guardrail. A percentage fee rewards the agency for growing spend, which is good when growth is profitable and bad when it is not. Tie budget increases to a minimum MER or contribution margin target so the agency only earns more when the business earns more.

### Should I choose an agency that only charges on performance?
Pure performance deals sound safe but depend on clean tracking and an agreed baseline. If attribution is disputed, the relationship suffers. Many brands prefer a hybrid, a modest base fee plus a performance component, which keeps the agency invested without arguments over every attributed sale.

### Does agency cost include creative production?
Often it does not. Some agencies only manage campaigns and expect you to supply footage, while others include strategy, editing and UGC sourcing. Ask how many new ads ship each month, who films them and whether creator fees and usage rights are inside the quote or billed separately.

### How long before an agency pays for itself?
Expect the first weeks to go on tracking, offer and creative foundations, with testing after that. Judge the agency on contribution margin and MER over roughly a quarter rather than on the first month, while watching early signals such as creative output, test velocity and the quality of reporting.

### Is an agency cheaper than hiring an in-house media buyer?
It depends on what you need. One in-house buyer costs a salary plus tools but rarely covers creative strategy, editing, CRO and email. An agency spreads those skills across a team. Compare the full cost of each option against the scope you need, not the salary against the fee.

### What spend level makes an agency worth it?
Agencies make most sense once you have product-market fit and enough budget to test properly. Our partners usually spend at least $10K to $20K a month on paid ads. Below that, the fee can take too large a share of the budget, so an audit or project often comes first.

# How to Scale Facebook Ads Without Breaking Your CPA
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/how-to-scale-facebook-ads
Summary: How to scale Facebook ads: 20 to 30% budget steps, horizontal scaling, Advantage campaign budget, cost caps and the creative volume that keeps CPA stable.

Direct Answer: How to scale Facebook ads profitably: raise budgets on proven campaigns in 20 to 30% steps every few days, expand winners into new audiences, placements and markets, and use cost caps or bid caps to protect CPA. The real lever is creative volume: a steady supply of new winning ads lets budget grow without efficiency collapsing.

      
      Vertical vs horizontal scaling: Vertical scaling raises the budget on a campaign that already works. Horizontal scaling spreads a winning formula into new campaigns, ads, audiences, placements or countries.

      
        
## When you are ready to scale Facebook ads

        Most guides on how to scale facebook ads start with budget tactics. The better starting point is whether the account deserves more money. Scaling multiplies whatever is already true: a profitable campaign becomes a bigger profitable campaign, and a leaky one loses money faster.
Check these conditions before you add budget. If two or more are missing, fix them first, because no bid strategy will cover a weak offer or broken tracking.

        - CPA has held at or below target for at least a week, not just for a lucky day or two.
- The campaign has exited the learning phase and delivery is stable.
- You know your break-even CPA and ROAS from real [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin).
- [Conversions API](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/conversions-api) is sending purchase events and match quality is healthy.
- You have inventory and fulfilment capacity for a higher order volume.
- At least three or four ads are carrying spend, not one hero ad.

        
        
      
        
## Vertical scaling: 20 to 30% budget steps

        Vertical scaling means raising the budget on a campaign that is already working. Large jumps can push Meta to find many more buyers overnight, and it reaches less likely ones to do it, so CPA often spikes. Steps of 20 to 30% every two to three days give delivery time to settle while still compounding quickly.
Example arithmetic: a campaign at $500 a day, raised 25% every other day, grows like this.

        
        DayDaily budgetChangeDay 1$500Starting budgetDay 3$625+25%Day 5$781+25%Day 7$977+25%Day 9$1,221+25%Day 11$1,526+25%
        
### Rules that keep vertical scaling safe
Judge each step on at least two or three days of data, not a single afternoon. If CPA rises more than your tolerance after a step, hold the budget instead of cutting it straight away. Cutting and raising repeatedly confuses delivery more than holding steady does.

      
        
## Horizontal scaling: more ads, audiences and markets

        Vertical scaling eventually hits a ceiling where each extra dollar buys fewer customers. Horizontal scaling raises that ceiling by giving Meta more ways to find buyers.

        - New creative concepts built on the winning angle, aimed at different buyer types.
- A duplicate of the winning campaign with a different bid strategy, such as a cost cap version next to a highest volume version.
- New placements, like Reels and Stories, using native vertical edits rather than cropped feed ads.
- New countries with similar buyers, such as the UK, Canada or Australia, once shipping and pricing are ready.
- Fresh landing pages or offers, such as a bundle, that open a new reason to buy.

        
        
      
        
## CBO and Advantage campaign budget

        Meta now calls campaign budget optimization Advantage campaign budget. You set one budget at campaign level and Meta moves money between ad sets toward the cheapest results. For scaling, that is usually what you want: fewer, broader ad sets with enough budget each, rather than many small ones competing for the same people.
Keep the structure simple. A typical scaling account has one Advantage+ sales campaign with the proven ads, one cost-controlled campaign for extra volume, and a separate testing campaign that feeds them. Ad set spend limits can stop Meta from starving a new ad set, but use them lightly, because heavy limits remove the reason to use a campaign budget at all.
When you raise an Advantage campaign budget, the same 20 to 30% rule applies. And because consolidation gives Meta's ranking system more room to choose, the quality and variety of ads inside the campaign matters more than the targeting around them.

        
        
        
      
        
## Cost caps and bid caps: scaling with a ceiling

        Highest volume bidding spends the whole budget and accepts whatever CPA the auction gives. That is fine at low spend, but at high spend it lets cost per purchase drift. Cost controls put a ceiling on what you will pay, which is why we add them once a brand moves into its scale phase.

        
        Bid strategyWhat it controlsUse it whenRiskHighest volumeNothing, spends the full budgetTesting and early scalingCPA drifts as spend risesCost per result goal (cost cap)Average CPA over timeYou know your target CPAUnder-delivery if the cap is too tightBid capMaximum bid in each auctionPeak periods and volatile CPMsVery low spend if set too lowROAS goalMinimum return on spendCatalogues with mixed pricesVolume drops when the goal is ambitious
        
### Manual bidding in practice
Set the first cap near your break-even CPA, with a budget several times higher than you expect to spend, then loosen the cap in small steps if delivery is too slow. A [jewelry brand](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies/apparel-fashion) we work with drove $54K in 7 days using [manual bidding](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/cases/why-your-facebook-ads-aren-scaling-fix-these-manual-bidding) campaigns at 4.43x ROAS.

      
        
## Creative volume is the real lever

        Budgets and bids decide how fast you spend. Creative decides how far you can go. Every ad has a pool of people it persuades, and as spend rises that pool runs dry: frequency climbs, CTR falls and CPA rises. The only lasting fix is more ads that reach different people for different reasons.
Meta's Andromeda retrieval system makes this stronger. It matches ads to people based on the creative itself, so ten similar ads behave like one, while ten distinct concepts open ten audiences. That is why our partner brands ship 30 to 50+ new creatives and angles a month and move toward 40+ assets a month once they are scaling.
Plan creative ahead of budget. Before each big step up, make sure the testing campaign has produced at least a few new winners ready to join the scaling campaigns.
Variety means more than new hooks on the same video. Mix formats such as [UGC](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/viral-creatives), founder clips, demonstrations, static images and carousels, and mix angles such as problem, result, comparison and gift. Each new combination gives Meta another route to a buyer who ignored your previous ads. The creative testing guide linked below covers how to find those winners without wasting budget.

        
        
        
      
        
## Signals to slow down or stop

        Scaling is not a one-way street. Pull back or hold when you see these patterns for more than a couple of days.
When a signal appears, diagnose before you cut. Check whether the cause is [creative fatigue](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/creative-fatigue), a tracking problem, a seasonal rise in CPMs or an issue on the store such as a stock-out or a slow page. Each one has a different fix, and cutting budget only treats the symptom.

        - CPA sits above target for three days in a row after a budget step.
- Frequency rises while CTR falls on your top ads, a classic sign of creative fatigue.
- CPMs climb and conversion rate drops at the same time.
- Platform ROAS holds but blended [MER](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/mer) in Shopify falls, meaning Meta is claiming sales it did not cause.
- The share of new customers in your orders drops, so you are mostly paying to reach existing buyers.
- Stock or fulfilment cannot keep up with the order volume.

        
        
      
        
## What scaling looks like on real accounts

        During Q4, one [dropshipping brand](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies/dropshipping-dtc) generated $133,420 in 7 days at 4.06x ROAS on $32,857 of spend. On a body contouring account, a disciplined scaling rule of thumb produced $19,977 in a day at 3.77x ROAS on $5,294 spend. Neither result came from one clever setting. They came from proven creative, budgets raised in steps and cost controls that kept CPA in range while spend grew.
If you want a second opinion before your next push, a [Meta ads audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/meta-ads-audit) or a full management engagement can map where your account's ceiling sits and what it will take to raise it.

        
        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### How much should I increase my Facebook ads budget at once?
Increase it by 20 to 30% every two to three days on campaigns that are already hitting target. Bigger jumps often push Meta to reach less likely buyers too quickly, which raises CPA. If a step pushes CPA past your tolerance, hold the budget for a few days instead of cutting it back immediately.

### Is horizontal or vertical scaling better?
You need both. Vertical scaling is faster and simpler on a proven campaign, but it hits a ceiling as the best audience gets saturated. Horizontal scaling, through new creative concepts, bid strategies, placements and countries, raises that ceiling. Most accounts scale vertically until efficiency slips, then expand horizontally.

### Do cost caps limit how much I can scale?
They limit spend when the auction gets expensive, which is the point. A cost cap set too tight will under-deliver, so start near break-even CPA with a generous budget and loosen it gradually. Many brands run a cost-capped campaign beside a highest volume campaign to get both volume and control.

### Why does ROAS drop when I scale Facebook ads?
At higher spend Meta has to reach people who are less ready to buy, and your best ads get shown to the same people more often. CPA rises as a result. Adding new creative concepts, raising budgets in steps and using cost controls slows that decline, and better offers or AOV can offset it.

### Should I duplicate winning ad sets to scale?
Duplicating can help when you want to test a different bid strategy or budget, but duplicates of the same ads in the same audience compete with each other. Prefer one consolidated campaign with a campaign budget, and use duplicates deliberately, for example a cost-capped copy of a proven campaign.

      
      
## Go deeper
- [Meta Andromeda Explained](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/meta-andromeda): Why creative diversity now decides who wins the auction.
- [Meta Ads Agency for Ecommerce](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/meta-ads-agency): Have the scaling campaigns and creative pipeline run for you.
- [Meta Ads Creative Testing](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/meta-ads-creative-testing): The testing system that feeds new winners into scale.
- [$133,420 in 7 Days at 4.06x](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/cases/q4-shaping-up-be-incredible-while-many-slow-down-weekend-ve): A Q4 scaling week on $32,857 of spend.

# TikTok Shop Strategy for DTC Brands: Listings to LIVE
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/tiktok-shop-strategy
Summary: A practical TikTok Shop strategy for DTC brands: listings, pricing, affiliate creators and samples, LIVE selling, Spark Ads, GMV Max and shop operations.

Direct Answer: A TikTok Shop strategy that works combines search-friendly product listings, pricing built for impulse buying, an affiliate creator program fuelled by free samples, regular LIVE sessions and paid amplification through Spark Ads and GMV Max. Behind it you need reliable fulfilment, because shop performance affects how much reach TikTok gives your products.

      
      TikTok Shop: TikTok's in-app store, where people buy products straight from videos, LIVE streams and the Shop tab without leaving the app. Sales can come from your own account, affiliate creators or ads.

      
        
## What a TikTok Shop strategy has to cover

        [TikTok Shop](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tiktok-shop-agency) is not a storefront you open and wait on. It is a loop: videos and LIVE streams create sales, sales and good reviews improve how TikTok ranks your products, and better ranking brings more creators and more reach. A TikTok Shop strategy has to keep every part of that loop turning at once.
That means six workstreams running in parallel: listings, pricing, affiliate creators, LIVE, paid amplification and operations. Brands that treat it as only a creator channel, or only an ad channel, usually stall, because the weak part of the loop slows everything else down.
Before you start, decide what TikTok Shop is for. For some brands it is a new customer acquisition channel that feeds the Shopify store. For others it is a sales channel in its own right. The answer changes how you price, which products you list and how much margin you can give creators.

        
        
        
      
        
## Product listings built for search and the feed

        Shoppers find products in the feed, in the Shop tab and through TikTok search. Your listing has to convert people who arrive from a 15-second video with almost no context.

        - Titles that use the words people search, such as the product type, main benefit and key attribute, rather than your internal product name.
- A first image that shows the product clearly on a clean background, followed by images of it in use, size references and what is in the box.
- A short product video on the listing itself, because many shoppers check it before buying.
- Complete attributes and categories so TikTok can match the product to searches and recommendations.
- Variants grouped on one listing where it makes sense, so reviews and sales build on a single page.
- A plan to earn early reviews, such as follow-up messages and sample programs, because a listing with no reviews converts poorly.

        
        
### Choose which products to list first
Start with one to three hero products that are easy to show on camera, priced for an impulse decision and strong enough on margin to pay creator commission. A focused catalogue concentrates sales and reviews, which helps ranking. Add the rest of the range once the first products have momentum and creators are asking for more.

      
        
## Pricing and offers for TikTok Shop

        TikTok Shop rewards impulse purchases, so pricing and offers carry more weight than on a typical Shopify store. But every sale has extra costs: platform fees, affiliate commission and often a promotional discount. Work out the margin before you set the price.
Example arithmetic only, using assumed rates rather than TikTok's actual fee schedule, which you should check for your market: a $40 product with $10 product cost, an assumed 8% platform fee, a 20% affiliate commission and $5 of shipping and packing.

        
        LineAmountSelling price$40.00Product cost-$10.00Platform fee (assumed 8%)-$3.20Affiliate commission (20%)-$8.00Shipping and packing-$5.00Contribution before ads$13.80
        
### Offers that suit TikTok Shop
- Bundles and multi-packs that raise order value and leave room for commission.
- Limited-time flash deals timed with LIVE sessions.
- A clear crossed-out price so the deal is obvious within a second of the video.

      
        
## Affiliate creators and samples

        For most brands, affiliate creators drive the bulk of TikTok Shop volume. Creators add your product to their showcase, post videos with a product link and earn a commission on each sale.
Start with an open collaboration so any eligible creator can promote the product at a set commission. Then run targeted collaborations with higher commissions for creators whose audience and past sales fit. Free samples are the main recruiting tool, so set approval rules: look at a creator's recent shop sales and content quality, not just follower count.
Every creator who gets a sample should also get a short brief: the problem the product solves, three hooks that have worked, what to show on camera and claims to avoid. Track which creators post after receiving a sample and which videos sell, then give your best creators higher commission, early access to new products and paid boosts. The recruiting and commission principles in our [DTC affiliate program](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/dtc-affiliate-program) guide apply here too.

        
        
        
      
        
## Selling on TikTok LIVE

        LIVE lets a host demonstrate the product, answer questions in real time and run deals that only exist during the stream. It suits products that need explaining or showing, such as skincare, gadgets and apparel.
Treat each LIVE as a show with a run-of-show plan: an opening hook, a demonstration, social proof, the offer, and a repeat of the offer every few minutes for people joining late. Pin the product, use flash deals with clear end times and have a second person handling comments. Consistency matters more than length, so a regular schedule your audience can learn beats occasional long streams. Clip the best moments into short videos afterwards so each LIVE also produces content.
Choose the host carefully. A founder or team member who knows the product and enjoys talking to an audience usually beats a scripted presenter. If no one on the team fits, some brands partner with experienced LIVE creators who host sessions for a commission. Review each stream afterwards: which moments drove orders, when viewers dropped and which questions came up repeatedly.

        
        
        
      
        
## Spark Ads and GMV Max

        Organic and affiliate content gets the loop started. Paid media makes it bigger. Two tools matter most for Shop sellers.

        
        ToolWhat it doesBest useSpark AdsRuns an existing organic or creator post as an ad, keeping its likes, comments and handleScaling creator videos that already sell organicallyGMV MaxTikTok's automated Shop campaign that optimises for total gross merchandise value across videos, LIVE and product cardsThe main paid engine for Shop products once you have content and sales history
        
### How to feed GMV Max
[GMV Max](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/tiktok-gmv-max) works with the content it can access, so its results depend on how many good videos exist for each product. Keep authorising strong creator posts, set a realistic return target based on your [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin) and give the campaign time to learn before judging it. Our GMV Max guide covers ROI targets, Max delivery and what to do when a campaign will not spend.

      
        
## Content cadence for your brand account and creators

        TikTok rewards consistency, and every video is another way into your products. A workable weekly rhythm looks like this.

        - Brand account: post short videos most days, mixing demonstrations, founder clips, customer questions and reposted creator content.
- Creators: aim for a steady flow of new affiliate videos every week, refilling samples as creators post.
- LIVE: hold sessions on a fixed schedule, and clip each one into shorter posts.
- Paid: review the week's top organic and creator videos every Monday and move the best into [Spark Ads](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tiktok-ads-agency) or GMV Max.
- Testing: try new hooks and angles weekly, borrowing what wins on TikTok for your Meta ads and the other way round.

        
        
      
        
## Operations that protect your shop

        TikTok scores shops on how well they serve customers, and a weak score can reduce reach and restrict features. Operations is a growth lever, not a back-office task.
Ship within the handling time TikTok requires and upload tracking quickly. Keep inventory synced with Shopify so you never sell stock you do not have. Answer customer messages fast, process returns and refunds cleanly and fix the causes of bad reviews, such as sizing confusion or damaged packaging. Where available, fulfilment by TikTok can take shipping off your plate. Finally, review compliance before you launch: product category rules and claims policies, especially for supplements and skincare, are stricter than many founders expect.

        
        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I get creators to promote my TikTok Shop products?
Set up an open collaboration with a competitive commission, then invite well-matched creators to targeted collaborations with free samples and a higher rate. Give each creator a short brief with proven hooks. Creators choose products that sell, so strong listings, good reviews and a clear offer make recruiting much easier.

### What commission should I offer TikTok Shop affiliates?
Work backwards from margin. Calculate contribution after product cost, platform fees, shipping and any discount, then decide how much you can share while still leaving room for ads and profit. Many brands run a base rate for open collaborations and a higher rate for proven creators who consistently drive sales.

### What is GMV Max on TikTok?
GMV Max is TikTok's automated campaign type for Shop sellers. It optimises for total gross merchandise value, choosing between your product videos, LIVE streams and product cards automatically. It performs best with plenty of good content per product and a return target based on your real contribution margin.

### Do I need to go LIVE to succeed on TikTok Shop?
No, but it helps for products that benefit from demonstration and questions. Many shops rely mainly on affiliate videos and ads. If you do go LIVE, a regular schedule, a clear run-of-show and exclusive flash deals matter more than long sessions, and every stream should be clipped into new short videos.

### Will TikTok Shop take sales away from my Shopify store?
Some customers who would have bought on Shopify will buy in-app instead, but TikTok Shop also reaches people who would never visit your site. Track total new customers and blended contribution margin across both channels, and price so that a TikTok Shop sale is still profitable after fees and commission.

# What Is a Good ROAS for Ecommerce? Break-Even by Margin
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/good-roas-for-ecommerce
Summary: What is a good ROAS? It depends on margin. See break-even ROAS by margin, new vs returning targets, platform vs blended ROAS and our published case data.

Direct Answer: What is a good ROAS? One that clears your break-even point with room for profit. Break-even ROAS equals 1 divided by your contribution margin before ad spend, so a brand with a 50% margin breaks even at 2x while a 30% margin brand needs 3.33x. A good target sits comfortably above that line.

      
      Break-even ROAS: The ROAS at which ad spend uses up all of the margin on a sale, leaving zero profit. It equals 1 divided by contribution margin before ad spend, written as a decimal.

      
        
## Why a good ROAS depends on your margin

        What is a good ROAS? Founders ask it as if there were one number, usually 3x or 4x. But the same 3x ROAS can be excellent for one brand and a slow cash leak for another. The difference is margin.
If you have not worked with the metric before, our guide to what ROAS is covers the formula and the basics. This post focuses on the next question: how high it needs to be for your brand.
ROAS measures revenue per dollar of ad spend. It says nothing about what that revenue costs to deliver. A brand that keeps 70 cents of every dollar after product cost, shipping and payment fees can afford to spend far more to win a sale than a brand that keeps 30 cents. So a good ROAS is not a benchmark you borrow. It is a number you calculate from your own unit economics, then adjust for customer type, campaign type and how you measure.

        
        
        
      
        
## Break-even ROAS by margin

        [Break-even ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator) is 1 divided by your [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin) before ad spend. Contribution margin here means what is left from each sale after product cost, shipping, packaging, payment fees and discounts. At break-even, ad spend uses up all of it.
The table below is calculated, not surveyed. The last column shows the ROAS needed to keep 15% of revenue as profit after ads, which is 1 divided by (margin minus 0.15).

        
        Contribution marginBreak-even ROASMargin on a $100 orderROAS for 15% profit after ads30%3.33x$306.67x40%2.50x$404.00x50%2.00x$502.86x60%1.67x$602.22x70%1.43x$701.82x
        
### What the table tells you
Low-margin brands have very little room. At 30% margin, a 4x ROAS only just covers costs, and real profit needs well over 6x. At 60% margin, 2.5x is already healthy. If your break-even is high, raising margin through bundles, price or product cost often helps more than chasing a higher ROAS.

      
        
## New vs returning customers

        First-order ROAS treats every customer as worth one purchase. If customers come back, you can accept a lower ROAS on the first order and still make money over time.
Example arithmetic only: AOV is $60 and contribution margin is 50%, so each order contributes $30. First-order break-even ROAS is 2x. If customers place an average of 1.8 orders in their first year, each customer contributes $54. You could pay up to $54 to acquire them and break even over the year, which is a first-order ROAS of $60 divided by $54, about 1.11x.
That does not mean you should run at 1.11x. Repeat revenue arrives later, so you fund the gap in cash, and repeat rates are estimates until you have cohort data. Most brands set a first-order target between break-even and the full lifetime figure, and they measure ROAS on new customers separately, because returning customers inflate the blended number.

        
        
        
      
        
## Prospecting vs retargeting ROAS

        [Retargeting campaigns](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/retargeting-for-dtc-brands) almost always report a higher ROAS than prospecting, because they reach people who already visited your store or added to cart. Many of those people would have bought anyway, so the ad gets credit for sales it did not fully create.
Prospecting campaigns find new buyers, so their ROAS looks lower while doing more of the real growth work. If you judge both against one target, you will move budget toward retargeting, the reported ROAS will rise and new customer growth will quietly stall.
Set separate expectations. Hold prospecting to a target based on new-customer economics, keep retargeting budgets small and capped, and judge the whole account on blended results. With broad [Advantage+ campaigns](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/advantage-plus) mixing both audiences, check the new versus existing customer split in your reporting.

        
        
        
      
        
## Platform ROAS vs blended ROAS

        Each ad platform reports the sales it believes it caused, using its own [attribution window](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/attribution-window). When a shopper sees a Meta ad, then searches on Google and buys, both platforms may claim the same order. Platform ROAS added together often overstates the truth.
Example arithmetic only: Meta reports $120,000 in revenue and Google reports $50,000, a combined $170,000 on $40,000 of total spend, or 4.25x. Shopify shows $140,000 in actual revenue. [Blended ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/blended-roas), also called [MER](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/mer), is $140,000 divided by $40,000, or 3.5x.
Use platform ROAS to compare campaigns and ads inside one platform. Use blended ROAS to decide whether the business is making money and whether to raise total budget. When the two drift apart, trust the one that matches your bank account.

        
        
        
      
        
## What ROAS looks like in our published case studies

        Across 25 published [case studies](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies) with a stated ROAS, the median is 3.97x. The middle half of results sits between 3.61x and 4.39x, and the full range runs from 2.06x to 11.6x. Treat these as success-biased: brands publish good months, not bad ones, so they show what strong performance looks like rather than an industry average.
Use the figures as context, not as a target. A [supplement brand](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies/supplements-nutrition) at 3.9x and a [dropshipping store](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies/dropshipping-dtc) at 11.6x tell you little about your own break-even line, because their margins, prices and repeat rates differ from yours. The useful lesson is that strong accounts across very different niches cluster around 3.5x to 4.5x on the campaigns they chose to publish, while their own margins decided whether that was a good result.

        
        NichePublished ROAS rangeSupplements3.89x to 4.51xFashion3.56x to 5.49xFitness3.61x to 4.37xSkincare3.64x to 4.39xDropshipping2.53x to 11.6xGeneral DTC2.06x to 3.8xJewelry4.43x
        
      
        
## When a lower ROAS is the right call

        A good ROAS is not always the highest one you can get. Sometimes accepting a lower number is the smarter move, as long as it is a deliberate decision with a time limit.
Launching a new product is one example. Early campaigns are buying data and reviews as well as sales, so a ROAS near break-even can be fine for a few weeks. Q4 is another: customers acquired in November can buy again in January, so brands with strong repeat rates often accept a lower first-order ROAS during the peak. Clearing old stock is a third, because recovering cash can matter more than margin.
The opposite also happens. A ROAS far above target can mean you are under-spending. If every campaign returns well above break-even, you are probably leaving profitable customers on the table, and a controlled budget increase is worth testing. Profit in dollars, not ROAS as a ratio, is what pays the bills.

        
        
        
      
        
## How to set your own good ROAS target

        Turn the ideas above into one working number in five steps.
Example arithmetic only: a brand with a $75 AOV keeps $33.75 per order after product cost, shipping, packaging and fees, a 45% margin. Break-even ROAS is 1 divided by 0.45, about 2.22x. To keep 10% of revenue as profit after ads, the target is 1 divided by 0.35, about 2.86x. That brand would treat anything under 2.2x as a loss and anything near 3x as healthy.

        - Calculate contribution margin per order after product cost, shipping, packaging, payment fees and average discount.
- Find break-even ROAS as 1 divided by that margin.
- Add the profit you need after ads to get a target ROAS for first orders.
- Adjust for repeat purchases using real cohort data, not hopes.
- Track blended ROAS weekly, and raise budgets only while it stays above target.

        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is a 2x ROAS good for ecommerce?
It depends on margin. A brand with a 60% contribution margin breaks even at 1.67x, so 2x is profitable. A brand with a 40% margin breaks even at 2.5x, so 2x loses money on every first order. Calculate your break-even ROAS as 1 divided by your margin before judging any number.

### Is a 4x ROAS good?
For most DTC brands, yes, but not all. At 50% margin, 4x leaves roughly 25% of revenue as profit after ads. At 30% margin, 4x barely clears break-even of 3.33x. It also depends on whether 4x is platform-reported or blended, since platform figures often overstate results.

### What is a good ROAS for Facebook ads?
A good Facebook ads ROAS is one above your break-even line that holds when checked against blended revenue. Our published case studies have a median of 3.97x, with the middle half between 3.61x and 4.39x, but those are success-biased. Your own margin decides what counts as good for you.

### Should retargeting have a higher ROAS target than prospecting?
Retargeting will naturally report a higher ROAS because it reaches people already close to buying, many of whom would buy anyway. Rather than a higher target, give it a small capped budget and judge it on incremental impact. Hold prospecting to a target based on new-customer economics.

### How do I calculate break-even ROAS?
Divide 1 by your contribution margin before ad spend, written as a decimal. If each $100 order leaves $40 after product cost, shipping, packaging and fees, the margin is 0.4 and break-even ROAS is 2.5x. Our break-even ROAS calculator does the arithmetic from your own numbers.

### Why is my blended ROAS lower than my Meta ROAS?
Meta, Google and other platforms each claim sales using their own attribution windows, so the same order can be counted more than once. Blended ROAS divides actual store revenue by total ad spend, which removes the double counting. A gap is normal, but a widening gap is a warning sign.

      
      
## Go deeper
- [What Is ROAS?](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/what-is-roas): The formula, ROAS vs ROI and the basics behind this guide.
- [Ecommerce ROAS Benchmarks](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/benchmarks/ecommerce-roas): ROAS figures from our published case studies by niche.
- [Break-Even ROAS Calculator](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator): Enter your margins to find your own break-even line.
- [Blended ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/blended-roas): Why total revenue over total spend is the number to trust.

# Shopify CRO Tips: A 10-Point Conversion Checklist
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/shopify-conversion-rate-optimization
Summary: Shopify CRO tips in one checklist: speed, above the fold, product pages, reviews, bundles, cart drawer, checkout, post-purchase, mobile and testing.

Direct Answer: The Shopify CRO tips that move revenue most are fast mobile load times, a clear offer above the fold, product pages that answer objections, visible reviews, bundles that lift order value, a cart drawer with upsells, a short checkout, post-purchase offers and a habit of testing one change at a time.

      
      Conversion rate optimization (CRO): The practice of increasing the share of visitors who buy, and how much they spend, by improving your store's speed, pages, offers and checkout based on data rather than opinion.

      
        
## The 10-point Shopify CRO checklist at a glance

        These [Shopify CRO](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/cro-agency) tips are ordered the way a shopper moves through your store, from the first second of loading to the thank-you page. Work through them in order, because a fix early in the journey affects every step after it. If your traffic comes mainly from paid social, most of it lands on mobile product pages, so start there.
Before changing anything, record your baseline for a few weeks: conversion rate by device and traffic source, add to cart rate, checkout completion rate, AOV and revenue per session. Without a baseline you cannot tell whether a change helped, and you risk keeping changes that only looked good during a strong sales week.

        
        AreaWhat good looks like1. SpeedPages load fast on a mid-range phone on mobile data2. Above the foldProduct, benefit, price, reviews and add to cart visible without scrolling3. Product pageAnswers the top objections before the shopper has to ask4. ReviewsStar rating near the title, photo reviews lower down5. Offers and bundlesA clear reason to buy more than one6. Cart drawerOpens on add to cart, shows progress to free shipping and one relevant add-on7. CheckoutExpress payment options and no surprise costs8. Post-purchaseOne-click upsell and a confirmation that builds trust9. MobileThumb-friendly buttons and a sticky add to cart10. TestingOne change at a time, judged on real orders
        
      
        
## Speed: the fix that helps every page

        A slow store loses shoppers before they see the product, and paid traffic is the least patient traffic you have. Test your key pages in PageSpeed Insights on mobile, and look at real-user data where it exists rather than desktop scores.

        - Remove apps you no longer use, because many leave scripts behind even after you stop using them.
- Compress images, serve modern formats and avoid giant hero videos above the fold.
- Load reviews, chat widgets and tracking scripts after the main content where possible.
- Use a lightweight, well-maintained theme rather than stacking customisations on an old one.
- Limit custom fonts to one or two weights.

        
        
### Check speed after every app install
Speed decays slowly as apps, sections and scripts pile up. Re-test your main product page whenever you add an app or a new section, and keep a short list of every script on the store and why it is there. Anything nobody can explain is a candidate for removal.

      
        
## Above the fold and the product page

        On a phone, the first screen decides whether someone scrolls or leaves. Show the product clearly, a one-line benefit, the price, the star rating and the add to cart button without any scrolling. Match the headline to the ad that sent the visitor, so the promise in the ad continues on the page.
Below the fold, the product page has one job: answer every objection before the shopper has to ask. List the questions customers send your support team and answer them on the page.

        - Who it is for and the result they can expect, in plain language.
- How to use it, with a short video or image sequence.
- Ingredients, materials, sizing or specifications, with a size guide where relevant.
- Shipping times, returns and guarantee close to the add to cart button.
- A comparison with the alternatives the shopper is weighing up.
- An FAQ section built from real customer questions.

        
        
      
        
## Reviews, offers and bundles

        Reviews do the selling a salesperson would do in a shop. Put the star rating and review count next to the product title, then show photo and video reviews further down, ideally filterable by concern, size or skin type. Ask for reviews in your post-purchase emails so the count keeps growing.
Offers and bundles raise order value, which means each visitor is worth more even if conversion rate stays the same. Quantity breaks such as buy two, save more suit consumables. Curated bundles suit routines and sets. A free gift above a spend threshold works well when the gift costs little but feels valuable. Show the saving clearly in money, not just as a percentage, and make the bundle the default choice where it suits most buyers.
Check margin before you launch any offer. A bundle that lifts AOV but gives away most of the profit on each order can raise revenue while lowering [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin). Work out the profit on each bundle option at its discounted price, and design the ladder so the option you want most buyers to choose is also the one that earns you the most.

        
        
        
      
        
## Cart drawer and checkout

        A cart drawer that slides open on add to cart keeps shoppers on the page and moving toward checkout. Use it well.

        - Show a progress bar toward free shipping, set just above your current AOV.
- Offer one relevant add-on, such as a refill or accessory, not a wall of products.
- Repeat the guarantee and delivery estimate.
- Make the checkout button the most obvious element in the drawer.

        
        
### Checkout
Shopify's checkout is already well optimised, so focus on what you control. Turn on express payment options such as Shop Pay, Apple Pay and Google Pay. Show shipping costs before checkout so there are no surprises. Keep discount code fields from sending shoppers off to hunt for codes, for example by applying offers automatically.

      
        
## Post-purchase and mobile

        The moment after purchase is the easiest time to sell more, because the customer has just decided to trust you. A one-click post-purchase upsell, shown before the thank-you page, adds revenue without touching conversion rate. Offer something that complements what they bought, at a modest discount, with no need to re-enter payment details. Then use the confirmation page and emails to set delivery expectations and reduce buyer's remorse.
Most paid social traffic is mobile, so review every step above on a real phone, not a desktop preview. Make buttons large enough for a thumb, add a sticky add to cart bar that appears on scroll, keep menus short, and check that pop-ups do not cover the product on small screens. Put a timer on your own checkout run: if it feels slow to you, it feels slower to a stranger.

        
        
        
      
        
## Testing changes the right way

        Change one thing at a time and measure it on real orders, not clicks. If traffic is high enough, run a proper A/B test. If it is not, make one change, keep traffic sources steady and compare a few weeks before and after, knowing the result is directional.
Small lifts are worth chasing. Example arithmetic only: a store with 20,000 monthly sessions and a $70 AOV.

        
        Conversion rateOrdersRevenue2.5%500$35,0003.0%600$42,0003.5%700$49,000
        
### Why this matters for ads
In that example, half a point of conversion rate adds $7,000 a month with no extra ad spend. It also lowers CPA on every campaign, which lets you scale budgets further before you hit your [break-even ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator).

      
        
## What this looks like on a real store

        When we rebuilt a clinical skincare store around this checklist, focusing on speed, product page structure, reviews and bundles, it reached a 5.25% store conversion rate and a $61,000 month. The work was not a redesign for its own sake. Each change answered a specific question: why do visitors leave, what do they need to see, and what would make them buy more than one.
Run through the ten points on your own store this week. Most brands find two or three gaps they can close quickly, and those quick fixes often matter more than any new campaign.

        
        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a good conversion rate for a Shopify store?
It varies with traffic source, price point and product, so compare against your own history rather than a general number. Paid social traffic usually converts lower than email or returning visitors. Track conversion rate by source and device, then judge each change by whether it lifts revenue per session.

### Which Shopify CRO tip should I start with?
Start with speed and the mobile product page, because most paid traffic lands there and every later step depends on it. Make sure the product, benefit, price, reviews and add to cart button are visible on the first screen of a phone, then work down the checklist in order.

### Do bundles really increase Shopify revenue?
They often raise average order value, which makes each visitor worth more even if conversion rate stays flat. Quantity breaks suit consumables and curated sets suit routines. Show the saving in money, make the bundle easy to choose and check that margin still works after the discount.

### Are post-purchase upsells worth adding?
Usually, yes. A one-click offer after payment adds revenue without risking the main conversion, because the customer has already bought. Keep it relevant to the first purchase, price it sensibly and avoid asking for payment details again. Measure take rate and any change in refunds.

### How do I A/B test on Shopify with low traffic?
With low traffic, a formal A/B test can take too long to reach a reliable answer. Make one change at a time, hold traffic sources steady and compare several weeks before and after. Prioritise changes with a clear reason behind them, such as answering a frequent customer question.

- [Shopify Agency](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/shopify-agency): The store build behind a 5.25% conversion rate and a $61,000 month.
- [Ecommerce CRO Agency](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/cro-agency): Have this checklist audited and implemented on your store.

# How to Scale a DTC Brand: A Stage-by-Stage Playbook
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/how-to-scale-a-dtc-brand
Summary: How to scale a DTC brand in stages: prove product-market fit, fix unit economics, add channels, build retention, then plan team and cash flow.

Direct Answer: How to scale a DTC brand comes down to fixing one constraint at a time: prove product-market fit, make unit economics repeatable so each new customer is profitable, then expand channels, build retention to raise lifetime value, and plan team and cash flow so growth does not outrun inventory or working capital. Skipping a stage usually stalls everything after it.

      
      Scaling a DTC brand: Growing revenue from direct-to-consumer sales faster than costs grow, so that each additional dollar of marketing and operations produces profitable new customers rather than just more volume.

      
        
## What scaling a DTC brand actually means

        Most founders asking how to scale a DTC brand mean one thing: how do I spend more on ads without the numbers falling apart. That is part of it, but ad spend is usually the last lever, not the first. Revenue that grows while [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin) shrinks is not scaling, it is buying a bigger problem.
Real scaling happens when the brand can add customers profitably and keep them. That depends on a chain of things: a product people want and come back for, margins that leave room to pay for acquisition, creative that keeps finding new buyers, more than one channel, and enough cash and people to fulfil the orders. Each link becomes the constraint at a different point in a brand's life.
After 12+ years in ecommerce and $50M+ in Meta ad spend managed, the pattern we see most often is a brand trying to solve a stage 2 problem with a stage 3 tactic, such as launching on TikTok or Google when Meta is unprofitable because the margins do not work. This guide walks through each stage, what to fix and what to measure, so you can work on the constraint that is actually holding you back.

        
        
        
      
        
## The five scaling stages at a glance

        Use this table to locate your brand. Most brands are mostly in one stage with a little overlap into the next. Work on the earliest stage where the measure is still weak.

        
        StageMain constraintWhat to fixWhat to measure1. Product-market fitDemand is unprovenOffer, positioning, product page, reviewsConversion rate, repeat rate, unprompted reviews2. Repeatable unit economicsEach customer costs too muchMargins, AOV, tracking, creative testingContribution margin per order, break-even ROAS, CAC3. Channel expansionOne channel caps outNew channels, new audiences, more creative volumeMER, new customer share, CAC by channel4. Retention and LTVCustomers buy onceEmail and SMS flows, subscriptions, cross-sellRepeat purchase rate, 90 and 180 day LTV5. Team and cash flowOperations and cashInventory planning, hiring, agency rolesCash conversion cycle, stockouts, payback period
        
      
        
## Stage 1: Product-market fit

        Before scaling, you need evidence that strangers want the product at a price that works. The signs are practical: people buy from cold traffic without heavy discounts, they leave reviews without being chased, some come back to reorder and the comments under your ads ask about the product rather than argue with it.
If those signs are missing, more spend just buys more expensive proof that the offer is not ready. Fix the basics first. Sharpen the positioning so the ad and the product page make one clear promise. Make the product page answer the questions buyers actually ask. Test the offer: bundles, a starter kit, a guarantee or a price point that changes perceived value.
This is also where tracking needs to be right. Without [Conversions API](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/conversions-api) and clean purchase events, you cannot tell whether a test worked. The typical clients we take on already have product-market fit and are doing about $20K a month or more, because before that point the work is mostly product and offer, not media buying.

        
        
        
      
        
## Stage 2: Repeatable unit economics

        Once demand is proven, the question becomes whether you can buy customers profitably, again and again. Start with contribution margin per order: revenue minus product cost, shipping, payment fees, returns and discounts. From that you get [break-even ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator), the minimum return each ad dollar must produce before you start losing money on the first order.
Then work on both sides of the equation. Raise what each order is worth with bundles, volume tiers and post-purchase upsells. Lower what each customer costs with better creative, which is the biggest lever on Meta and TikTok today, and a store that converts more of the traffic you already pay for. One clinical skincare store we worked with reached a 5.25 percent conversion rate in a $61,000 month after product page and checkout work, which changed what it could afford to spend per click.
Creative testing becomes a system at this stage. Our partner brands typically get 30 to 50+ new ad creatives and angles a month, built from a hook and angle matrix so each test teaches something. Our guides on Meta ads creative testing and lowering CAC go deeper on both.

        - Know your break-even ROAS and target ROAS before raising budget.
- Track contribution margin weekly, not only revenue and ROAS.
- Test offers and AOV levers alongside creative, not after.

        
        
      
        
## Stage 3: Channel expansion

        When Meta is profitable and stable, scale it first. It is usually cheaper to grow a channel that already works than to open a new one. Raise budgets in steps of about 20 to 30 percent, use cost caps where volume allows and keep feeding new creative so the account does not fatigue. Our guide on how to scale Facebook ads covers the budget mechanics.
Add channels when the main one starts to cap out: CAC rising faster than budget, frequency climbing, or new customer share falling. The usual next steps for DTC brands are TikTok, through in-feed ads, [Spark Ads](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tiktok-ads-agency) and [TikTok Shop](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tiktok-shop-agency) with creator affiliates, and Google, through Shopping, [Performance Max](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/google-shopping-ads-agency) and brand search to capture the demand that social creates. New markets such as the UK, Canada or Australia are another form of expansion once fulfilment and currency are sorted.
Some of our case results came from this stage. A UK [skincare brand](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies/skincare-beauty) generated EUR 118,000 in its first month with us, and one DTC brand reached $2.3M in sales at 11.6x ROAS on $200K of Meta spend over a year. Neither number is typical, and both depended on the earlier stages already working. Judge expansion on blended [MER](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/mer) and total new customers, not on each platform's own report.

        
        
        
      
        
## Stage 4: Retention and lifetime value

        Acquisition gets harder as you scale because you move past the easiest buyers. Retention is what lets you keep paying more for each new customer without losing money, because each one is worth more over time.
Start with the owned channels. [Klaviyo email](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/klaviyo-email-sms-agency) and SMS flows (welcome, abandonment, post-purchase, replenishment and win-back) should be live and tested before you push spend hard. Then add structural reasons to return: subscriptions or subscribe and save for consumables, refill reminders timed to real usage, a product range that gives buyers a logical second purchase, and loyalty perks that cost less than a discount.
Measure LTV by cohort, for example the revenue per customer 90 and 180 days after their first order, and compare it with what you paid to acquire them. When that ratio improves, you can afford higher CAC targets, which means more room to scale on paid social. Our LTV calculator and the ecommerce email flows guide are good starting points.

        
        
        
      
        
## Stage 5: Team and cash flow

        Many profitable DTC brands stall not because the ads stop working but because the business runs out of cash or capacity. Inventory has to be paid for weeks or months before it sells, ad platforms bill quickly and a strong month can empty the warehouse. Plan inventory against your spend plan, keep a buffer for peak periods such as [BFCM](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/bfcm-meta-ads-playbook) and Q4, and know your payback period so you can see how long each new customer takes to return their acquisition cost.
The team question is about roles, not headcount. Someone has to own media buying, creative production, the store, retention and operations. Early on that is often the founder plus freelancers. As spend grows, brands usually choose between hiring in-house specialists and working with an agency, or a mix. Our comparison of agency versus in-house media buyers covers the trade-offs, and the guide to DTC agency costs explains the common pricing models.
Scaling also raises the cost of mistakes. A tracking error at $2,000 a day is annoying; at $20,000 a day it is expensive. Weekly reporting on contribution margin, MER and cash keeps decisions grounded as volume rises.

        
        
        
      
        
## Common scaling mistakes

        These are the patterns we see most often when brands come to us for a [Brand Growth Audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/book). Each one is fixable, but each one also wastes months if it goes unnoticed.

        - Raising budgets based on platform ROAS while contribution margin quietly falls.
- Launching new channels to escape a creative or offer problem on the main channel.
- Running the same few ads for months and blaming the algorithm when performance drops.
- Leaning on discounts to hit revenue targets, which trains customers to wait for sales.
- Ignoring retention until acquisition costs force the issue.
- Ordering inventory without linking it to the ad spend plan, leading to stockouts at peak.
- Measuring each channel in isolation instead of tracking blended MER and new customer growth.

        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### When is a DTC brand ready to scale?
When cold traffic converts at a price that leaves a healthy contribution margin, customers leave reviews and some reorder, and tracking is reliable enough to trust test results. If you need deep discounts to sell or every campaign is below break-even ROAS, fix the offer, product page and margins before raising spend.

### What is the fastest way to scale a DTC brand?
Scale the channel that already works before adding new ones, and feed it more creative. For most DTC brands that means Meta, with budgets raised in steps of about 20 to 30 percent and a steady supply of new ads. Speed comes from fixing the current constraint, not from launching everything at once.

### How much should a DTC brand spend on ads to scale?
Work backwards from margins instead of picking a number. Calculate break-even ROAS from contribution margin, set a target CAC that your first order or 90 day LTV can support, then raise spend while blended MER stays above target. Our typical clients spend at least $10K to $20K a month on paid ads when we start.

### Should I add TikTok or Google before scaling Meta further?
Usually not. If Meta is profitable but not yet capped, more creative and budget there is cheaper than opening a new channel. Add TikTok or Google when Meta CAC rises faster than spend, frequency climbs or new customer share drops. Google brand search and Shopping also help capture demand that social ads create.

### Why does ROAS drop when I scale?
As budgets grow, platforms reach beyond your most likely buyers, so each extra dollar finds slightly less ready customers. Creative fatigue and audience overlap add to it. Some decline is normal. Judge it against break-even ROAS and blended MER, and offset it with new creative, better conversion rate, higher AOV and stronger retention.

### Do I need an agency to scale a DTC brand?
No, but you need the skills an agency provides: media buying, creative production, CRO, retention and reporting. Some brands hire in-house, others use an agency or a mix. The right choice depends on spend level, how fast you need results and whether you can recruit and manage specialists yourself.
