# Ecommerce Profit Margin: Gross, Contribution and Net Margin per Order
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/ecommerce-profit-margin
Summary: Ecommerce profit margin explained per order: gross, contribution and net margin, every cost line, a worked example and how margin sets break-even ROAS.

Direct Answer: Ecommerce profit margin is the share of each order you keep after costs. Gross margin subtracts only product cost, contribution margin also subtracts shipping, fulfilment and payment fees, and net margin per order then subtracts ad cost, returns and discounts. Contribution margin is the one that sets your break-even CPA and ROAS.

      
      Ecommerce profit margin: The percentage of revenue a store keeps as profit. For a DTC brand it is most useful per order, measured at three levels: gross margin (after product cost), contribution margin (after all variable costs of fulfilling the order) and net margin (after ad cost, returns and discounts too).

      
        
## Why measure ecommerce profit margin per order

        Ecommerce profit margin is usually discussed as one number on a yearly profit and loss statement. That is useful for your accountant and nearly useless for running ads. By the time the annual figure tells you something went wrong, you have spent months buying orders that lost money.
For a DTC brand, the more useful view is margin per order. Every order carries the same set of costs: the product, getting it to the customer, the payment fee, the ad spend it took to win it and a share of returns and discounts. If you know those numbers for a typical order, you know what you can afford to pay for a customer, which campaigns are really profitable and which levers will move profit the most.
This guide breaks margin into three levels, walks through each cost line, works through a full example and shows how margin turns into the [break-even ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator) your ads have to beat. It does not quote industry averages, because margins vary so much by product, price and channel that an average tells you very little about your own store.

        
        
        
      
        
## Gross vs contribution vs net margin

        The three margins answer different questions. Gross margin tells you whether the product is priced well against what it costs to make. [Contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin) tells you how much each order leaves to pay for marketing and overhead. Net margin per order tells you what you actually keep once marketing, returns and discounts are paid.

        - Fixed overhead such as salaries, software and rent sits below all three. It is paid from the total net profit of all orders, not from any single one.
- Some teams call the figure after ad cost "contribution margin after marketing". The label matters less than using the same definition every week.

        MarginFormula per orderWhat it tells youGross margin(Price minus COGS) divided by priceWhether pricing covers product cost with room to spareContribution margin (before ads)Price minus COGS, shipping and fulfilment, and payment feesThe most you can spend to acquire the order and break evenNet margin per orderContribution margin minus ad cost per order, returns and discounts, divided by priceWhat each order really earns before fixed overhead
        
      
        
## The cost lines that eat your margin

        Most margin mistakes come from leaving a cost out, not from bad arithmetic. List every line below for your top products, using real invoices and platform reports rather than estimates.

        - COGS: the landed cost of the product, including manufacturing, packaging, inbound freight and duties.
- Shipping and fulfilment: postage, pick and pack fees, packaging materials and any free shipping you absorb.
- Payment fees: the percentage and fixed fee your payment processor and any buy now, pay later provider charges per order.
- Ad cost per order: total ad spend divided by orders, which is your blended cost per acquisition.
- Returns: refunded revenue, return shipping and any stock you cannot resell, spread across all orders.
- Discounts: every code, sale price and automatic offer, which come straight off the price before any cost is covered.

        
        
      
        
## Worked example: margin on a $70 order

        This is an example, not a benchmark. It uses a $70 order with $21 COGS, $8 shipping and fulfilment, a 3 percent payment fee, a $25 ad cost per order and a 6 percent return rate. To keep it simple, returns are treated as full refunds, so the expected return cost per order is 6 percent of $70, or $4.20. There is no discount in this example.

        
        Line (example)Per orderRunning totalPrice$70.00$70.00COGSminus $21.00$49.00 (gross margin 70.0%)Shipping and fulfilmentminus $8.00$41.00Payment fee (3% of $70)minus $2.10$38.90 contribution before adsAd cost per order (CPA)minus $25.00$13.90Returns (6% of $70)minus $4.20$9.70 net profit per orderNet margin$9.70 divided by $7013.9%
        
### What the example shows
A 70 percent gross margin looks healthy, yet the order keeps only $9.70, a 13.9 percent net margin. Ad cost is by far the largest line after COGS. That is typical of paid-acquisition DTC brands and is why the ad cost per order deserves as much attention as product cost.

      
        
## How margin sets your break-even ROAS

        Your contribution margin is the most you can pay in ads for an order before it loses money. Divide price by that margin and you get break-even ROAS: the [return on ad spend](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/what-is-roas) at which ads exactly pay for themselves.
In the example, contribution before ads is $38.90, so break-even ROAS is $70 divided by $38.90, or 1.80x. If you also take the $4.20 expected return cost out first, the margin available for ads is $34.70 and break-even ROAS rises to 2.02x. The actual ROAS at a $25 CPA is $70 divided by $25, or 2.80x, which is why the order is profitable.
The lower your margin, the higher the ROAS your ads must reach. This is why two brands can run the same ROAS and get very different results: one is profitable and the other loses money on every order. Our break-even [ROAS calculator](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/roas-calculator) does this for your own numbers, and our guides to what ROAS is and [what a good ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/good-roas-for-ecommerce) for ecommerce looks like explain how to set a target above break-even.

        
        
        
      
        
## How to raise your margin

        There are only a few ways to make each order more profitable: earn more per order, spend less to deliver it, spend less to acquire it or earn more from the customer later. These are the levers we work on most often with partner brands.

        
        
        
### Raise average order value
Shipping, fulfilment and a large part of acquisition cost are roughly fixed per order, so a bigger basket spreads them further. Post-purchase upsells, cart add-ons and tiered offers all lift AOV without raising your cost to acquire the order.

### Use bundles
Bundles of products that are often bought together raise order value and let you offer a clear saving without discounting single items. They also give you a better offer for paid traffic than a percentage code.

### Fix shipping costs
In the example, $8 of shipping is 11.4 percent of a $70 order. On a $100 order with the same shipping cost, it would be 8 percent. Set a free shipping threshold above your current AOV, renegotiate carrier rates and check packaging size and weight.

### Improve conversion rate
CRO lowers ad cost per order without touching the budget. If the same traffic converts better, every order costs less to acquire. Faster pages, clearer product pages and a simpler checkout are usually where the gains are.

### Build retention
A repeat order through email or SMS carries almost no ad cost, so its net margin is close to its contribution margin. [Klaviyo flows](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/klaviyo-email-sms-agency) for replenishment, cross-sell and win-back raise lifetime margin even when first-order margin is thin.

      
        
## Profit margins in our published cases

        Instead of quoting averages, here are three real results from our published [case studies](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies) where the brand reported its profit margin. Each is a single account and a specific period, and each brand defines margin its own way, so treat them as examples of what is possible, not as targets.
A [dropshipping store](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/case-studies/dropshipping-dtc) generated $185,936 in 21 days at a 56 percent profit margin, covered in our case study on scaling that store. Another brand did $148K in one day and a $294K month while ending at a 37 percent net margin, in our case study on its best day. A third spent $26,594 to generate $99,576 in 5 days at a 67 percent profit margin, in our five-day case study.
What these share is that margin was tracked during the scale, not checked afterwards. Spend went up on products and offers where the numbers held, which is the habit this guide is built around. You can find all three on our case studies page.

        
        
        
      
        
## Track margin weekly, not yearly

        Build a simple weekly sheet with revenue, orders, COGS, shipping, fees, ad spend, refunds and discounts. Work out contribution margin per order and net profit per order each week, alongside [blended ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/blended-roas) or [MER](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/mer). When net profit per order falls, the sheet shows you which line moved.
Review it per product as well as per store, because a bestseller with thin margins can hide behind a healthy store average. Recheck COGS and shipping whenever a supplier or carrier changes prices, and recheck ad cost per order whenever you raise budget. Our profit margin calculator gives you the per-order figures, and the contribution margin glossary entry explains the definition in more detail.

        
        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is a good ecommerce profit margin?
There is no single good number, because margin depends on product, price, channel and how much you spend on ads. A better test is whether your contribution margin leaves enough room to acquire customers at your current cost per order and still keep a net profit. Work out your own figures per order instead of comparing with averages.

### What is the difference between gross margin and contribution margin?
Gross margin subtracts only the cost of goods from the price. Contribution margin also subtracts the other variable costs of each order, such as shipping, fulfilment and payment fees. Contribution margin is more useful for ads because it shows the most you can spend to acquire an order before it loses money.

### How do I calculate net profit margin per order?
Start with price, subtract COGS, shipping and fulfilment and payment fees to get contribution margin, then subtract ad cost per order, returns and discounts. Divide what is left by the price. In the $70 example in this guide, net profit is $9.70 per order, a 13.9 percent net margin before fixed overhead.

### Should returns be included in profit margin?
Yes. Returns cost you refunded revenue, return shipping and sometimes stock you cannot resell. Spread the expected cost across all orders using your return rate. A simple method treats returns as full refunds, so a 6 percent return rate on a $70 order adds $4.20 of cost to every order.

### How does profit margin affect break-even ROAS?
Break-even ROAS equals price divided by contribution margin. A lower margin means each order can afford less ad spend, so ads must return more revenue per dollar to break even. In the example in this guide, a $38.90 contribution margin on a $70 order gives a 1.80x break-even ROAS.

### What is the fastest way to improve ecommerce margin?
It depends on which cost line is largest. For most paid-acquisition DTC brands, ad cost per order is the biggest lever, so improving conversion rate and creative often moves margin fastest. Raising AOV with bundles and upsells, setting a smarter free shipping threshold and building repeat purchases through email and SMS follow close behind.

      
      
## Go deeper
- [Profit Margin Calculator](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/profit-margin-calculator): Enter price and costs to see gross, contribution and net margin per order.
- [What Is Contribution Margin?](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin): The margin that tells you what each order can afford to spend on ads.
- [Break-Even ROAS Calculator](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator): Turn your margin into the ROAS your ads need to make money.
- [$185,936 in 21 Days at 56% Margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/cases/185936-21-days-56-profit-margin-scaled-dropshipping-store-beyond): A store scaled while keeping profit margin in view.

# Meta Ads Learning Phase: What It Is, Learning Limited and How to Exit It
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/meta-ads-learning-phase
Summary: The Meta ads learning phase explained: the 50 conversions per week rule, what Learning Limited means, what resets learning and how to budget your way out.

Direct Answer: The Meta ads learning phase is the period after you launch or significantly edit an ad set when Meta is still working out who to show it to. Meta says an ad set generally needs about 50 optimization events within 7 days of its last significant edit to exit learning. If it is not on track to get there, Meta labels it Learning Limited.

      
      Meta ads learning phase: The period when Meta's delivery system is exploring the best people, placements and times to show a new or significantly edited ad set. Performance is less stable and cost per result is usually higher until the ad set collects enough optimization events, which Meta puts at roughly 50 in 7 days.

      
        
## What is the Meta ads learning phase?

        The Meta ads learning phase is the stretch of time after an ad set launches, or after a significant edit, when Meta's delivery system is still testing who to show your ads to. You will see "Learning" in the Delivery column of Ads Manager while it happens.
During this period Meta spends part of your budget exploring different people, placements and times of day, and uses the results to predict who is most likely to take the action you optimize for, such as a purchase. Until it has enough results, delivery is less stable and cost per result is usually higher and more volatile.
Learning happens at the ad set level. Each ad set learns on its own, even when several sit inside the same campaign. That detail matters for DTC brands, because the most common reason an account never leaves learning is a budget split across too many ad sets for any one of them to collect enough data.

        
        
        
      
        
## The 50 conversions per week rule

        Meta's documented guideline is that an ad set generally needs about 50 optimization events within 7 days of its last significant edit to exit the learning phase. An optimization event is whatever conversion the ad set is set to optimize for. For most ecommerce ad sets that is a purchase, so in practice the rule reads as roughly 50 purchases per ad set per week.
Two parts of that rule are easy to miss. First, it counts events for the ad set, not the campaign or the account. Ten ad sets with 10 purchases each add up to 100 purchases a week, but none of them is close to exiting learning. Second, the 7-day window restarts after every significant edit, so an ad set that keeps getting changed keeps starting over. Meta describes 50 as a guide rather than a hard switch, so treat it as the planning target and check the Meta Business Help Center if your account shows something different.

        
        
        
      
        
## How long is the Facebook learning phase?

        The Facebook learning phase lasts until the ad set collects about 50 optimization events, and Meta gives it a 7-day window from the last significant edit to get there. With a large enough budget, an ad set can leave learning in two or three days. With a small budget, it may never leave.
So the honest answer to "how long" is that it depends on your budget and your cost per result, not on the calendar. An ad set spending enough to buy 15 purchases a day will usually exit learning within about four days. An ad set buying three purchases a day will collect about 21 in a week and stay stuck. Plan for this before launch: if your budget cannot buy about 50 events a week, change the structure or the optimization event first.

        
        
        
      
        
## What Learning Limited means

        Learning Limited means Meta expects the ad set will not get enough optimization events to exit the learning phase. It is a status, not a penalty. Your ads keep delivering, but Meta is telling you that the ad set is unlikely to reach stable performance with its current setup.
When you hover over the status in Ads Manager, Meta usually suggests a cause. The common ones are:

        - Budget too low for the cost of the optimization event.
- Audience too small, often from stacked interests, tight age or location limits or heavy exclusions.
- A cost cap, [bid cap](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/cases/why-your-facebook-ads-aren-scaling-fix-these-manual-bidding) or ROAS goal set so tight that Meta cannot win enough auctions.
- Too many ad sets in the account competing for similar people, so each gets a thin slice of the results.
- An optimization event that is too rare, such as purchases on a product that sells only a few times a week.

        
        
### Is Learning Limited always bad?
Not always. A small [retargeting](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/retargeting-for-dtc-brands) ad set or a test ad set with a deliberate budget can sit in Learning Limited and still be profitable. The status only says the ad set is not getting enough events for Meta's system to optimize fully. If the ad set hits your target CPA consistently, you do not have to fix it. If it is your main prospecting ad set and results swing from day to day, you should.

      
        
## What resets the learning phase

        A significant edit resets the learning phase and restarts the 7-day window. Meta treats the following as significant edits:

        - Changing targeting, including audiences, locations, age ranges and Advantage+ audience settings.
- Changing creative, or adding a new ad to the ad set.
- Changing the optimization event, for example from purchase to add to cart.
- Changing the bid strategy or making a large change to a bid, cost cap or ROAS goal.
- Making a large budget change on the ad set, or on the campaign when you use Advantage campaign budget.
- Pausing the ad set for 7 days or longer and then turning it back on.

        
        
### What Meta does not publish
Meta does not publish an exact percentage at which a budget change becomes significant. Advice such as "raise budgets by no more than 20 percent" is a rule of thumb from practitioners, not Meta's rule. Small, spaced changes are less likely to reset learning than one large jump, which is why gradual increases are the safe default. Small edits such as fixing a typo in ad copy may or may not count, so batch your edits and make them together rather than one at a time over several days.

      
        
## How to size a budget that can exit learning

        Set the daily budget of each ad set to at least your expected cost per optimization event, times 50, divided by 7. That is the spend needed to buy about 50 events in a week. If your ad set's budget is below that number, it is unlikely to exit learning.
Daily budget needed = expected CPA x 50 / 7.
Worked example: a DTC brand sells a $60 product and expects a cost per purchase of about $30 from prospecting. $30 times 50 is $1,500 a week, and $1,500 divided by 7 is about $214 a day, so round up to $215. The table shows how different structures with the same CPA compare. These are illustrative numbers, not benchmarks.

        - The four-ad-set account spends $240 a day and buys about 56 purchases a week in total, but each ad set only sees about 14, so all four stay in learning.
- Moving the same $240 into one ad set gets that ad set past 50 without spending a dollar more.
- CPA during learning is usually higher than the stable CPA, so budget 20 to 30 percent above the formula if you can. In this example that is roughly $260 to $280 a day.

        Setup (example)Daily budget per ad setWeekly spend per ad setEvents per ad set per weekEnough to exit learning?One ad set optimizing for purchase, $30 CPA$90$63021 purchasesNoFour ad sets at $60 a day each, $30 CPA$60$42014 purchasesNo, in any of themThe same $240 a day in one ad set, $30 CPA$240$1,68056 purchasesYesBudget from the formula, $30 CPA$215$1,50550 purchasesJust, with no bufferOne ad set optimizing for add to cart, $9 per add to cart$65$45550 add to cartsYes, for that event
        
### Check the budget against your margin
The formula tells you what learning needs. It does not tell you whether that CPA is profitable. Before raising budget to hit 50 a week, check that your expected CPA sits below your break-even CPA. Our [break-even ROAS calculator](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator) turns your price and costs into that limit, and the Meta ads budget calculator works out the daily budget for a target number of purchases.

      
        
## How DTC brands get out of the learning phase

        To exit the learning phase, give each ad set more optimization events per week: fewer ad sets, broader audiences, enough budget and fewer edits. If even that cannot reach 50 a week, temporarily optimize for a more frequent event. These are the moves that work most often in DTC accounts.

        
        
        
### Consolidate ad sets
Merge ad sets that target similar people or test small variations. Put several creatives in one ad set instead of one creative per ad set, and let Meta spread delivery across them. Consolidation is the fastest fix because it raises events per ad set without raising total spend, as the worked example shows.

### Use broader audiences
Narrow interest stacks and tight lookalikes limit how many people Meta can reach at a reasonable cost. Broad targeting or Advantage+ audience gives the system more room to find buyers, which usually brings more events for the same budget. Keep exclusions for recent purchasers, but avoid stacking so many conditions that the audience shrinks to a few hundred thousand people.

### Optimize for a higher-funnel event for a while
If your budget cannot buy 50 purchases a week, optimize for an event that happens more often, such as add to cart or initiate checkout, until purchase volume grows. In the example, 50 add to carts a week need about $65 a day instead of $215. The trade-off is that Meta then finds people who add to cart, not necessarily people who buy, so watch cost per purchase closely and switch back to purchase optimization once you can afford it. Remember that switching the event is itself a significant edit.

### Stop editing during learning
Every significant edit restarts the clock. Decide what you will change before launch, then leave the ad set alone for at least three to five days unless it is clearly losing money. Judge results on the full week, not on the first day, when learning makes costs noisy.

### Fix tracking first
If purchases are not reaching Meta reliably, the ad set learns from fewer events than you actually sold. Check that the Meta pixel and the [Conversions API](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/conversions-api) are both sending purchase events and that event match quality is healthy before you blame the budget.

      
        
## How to scale budgets without resetting learning

        The safest way to scale without resetting learning is to raise budgets in small, spaced steps on ad sets that are already out of learning and profitable. When you need a bigger jump than that, duplicate or move spend into a consolidated campaign instead of making one large edit to a winner.

        
        
        
### Gradual budget increases
Raise the budget of a stable ad set by a modest amount, many teams use about 20 to 30 percent, then wait two or three days before the next step. This is a rule of thumb rather than a Meta threshold, but it keeps each change small enough that delivery usually stays stable. If CPA rises above target after a step, hold the budget there until it settles.

### Duplicating an ad set
Duplicating a winning ad set at a higher budget leaves the original untouched, so its learning is not reset. The copy starts its own learning phase, though, and it competes in the same auctions as the original, which can raise costs for both. Use duplication for one clear step up, not as a habit that fills the account with near-identical ad sets.

### Advantage campaign budget and Advantage+ sales campaigns
With Advantage campaign budget, previously called campaign budget optimization or CBO, you set one budget at campaign level and Meta shifts spend between ad sets. That makes it easier for the strongest ad set to collect enough events. Advantage+ sales campaigns, previously Advantage+ shopping campaigns, go further by consolidating targeting and placements into one unit, which suits brands that want fewer, bigger ad sets. A large change to the campaign budget can still count as a significant edit, so the same rule of gradual steps applies. Our Meta Advantage+ guide covers when this structure fits.

      
        
## When learning is not the real problem

        Sometimes an ad set exits learning and still loses money, or stays in learning because nobody wants the offer. Learning is about how stable delivery is, not about whether the product, price or creative can sell.
If you have consolidated, broadened and funded an ad set properly and CPA is still above break-even, look at the creative, the offer and the landing page before touching structure again. More events will not fix a weak hook or an unclear product page. Our guide to Meta ads creative testing explains how to find new winners without breaking learning on the ads that already work, and our guide to what ROAS is covers how to set the target your ads need to hit.
If you want a second pair of eyes on an account that never seems to leave learning, our [Meta ads agency](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/meta-ads-agency) team can review the structure, tracking and budgets and show you where the events are being split.

        
        
        
      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the learning phase in Meta ads?
It is the period after an ad set launches or is significantly edited when Meta is still testing who to show the ads to. Performance is less stable and cost per result is usually higher. The ad set exits learning once it collects about 50 optimization events within 7 days of its last significant edit.

### How many conversions do you need to exit the learning phase?
Meta's guideline is about 50 optimization events per ad set within 7 days of the last significant edit. For an ad set optimizing for purchases, that means roughly 50 purchases a week in that one ad set. Events in other ad sets in the same campaign do not count toward it.

### How long is the Facebook learning phase?
It lasts until the ad set reaches about 50 optimization events, with a 7-day window from the last significant edit. A well-funded ad set can exit in two or three days. An ad set whose budget buys only a few events a day may never exit and will be labelled Learning Limited.

### How do I fix Learning Limited?
Give the ad set more events per week. Consolidate similar ad sets, broaden the audience, loosen any cost cap or bid cap that is too tight and set the daily budget to at least your expected CPA times 50 divided by 7. If that is not affordable, optimize for a more frequent event such as add to cart for a while.

### Does changing the budget reset the learning phase?
A large budget change can, on the ad set or on the campaign when you use Advantage campaign budget. Meta does not publish an exact threshold. Many advertisers raise budgets by about 20 to 30 percent at a time and wait a few days between steps, which usually keeps delivery stable.

### Should I duplicate an ad set to scale it?
It can be useful for one clear step up, because the original ad set keeps its learning. The duplicate starts learning from scratch and competes with the original in the same auctions. For ongoing scaling, gradual budget increases on the winner or a consolidated Advantage campaign budget setup are usually cleaner.

      
## Sources
- About the learning phase (Meta Business Help Center)
- Last significant edit (Meta Business Help Center)
- View campaign, ad set or ad delivery status in Meta Ads Manager (Meta Business Help Center)

# TikTok Shop vs Shopify: Which Should a DTC Brand Sell On?
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/tiktok-shop-vs-shopify
Summary: TikTok Shop vs Shopify compared on checkout, traffic, fees, customer data, creators and fulfilment, and when a DTC brand should run both together.

Direct Answer: TikTok Shop and Shopify are not really either-or. Shopify is your own store: you own the checkout and the customer relationship, but you have to bring the traffic. TikTok Shop is a marketplace inside TikTok: it brings shoppers and creators, but takes a fee per order and controls the customer data. Most DTC brands are best served using Shopify as the hub and TikTok Shop as a sales channel.

      
      TikTok Shop vs Shopify: A comparison between selling inside TikTok, where shoppers buy without leaving the app and TikTok runs the checkout, and selling on your own Shopify store, where you run the checkout, set the experience and keep the customer relationship but must drive the traffic yourself.

      
        
## TikTok Shop vs Shopify: the short answer

        If you can only pick one, pick Shopify when you want to own the brand, the customer list and the margin, and pick [TikTok Shop](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tiktok-shop-agency) when your product sells on impulse from short videos and you need demand more than control. For most DTC brands that already have a store, the better question is not which one but how to run TikTok Shop as a channel without hurting the store.
The two do different jobs. Shopify is infrastructure: a store, a checkout and a back office that you control. TikTok Shop is a marketplace with its own audience, its own checkout and its own rules. Comparing them is closer to comparing your own website with Amazon than comparing two website builders.

        
        
        
      
        
## What TikTok Shop and Shopify actually are

        TikTok Shop is an ecommerce marketplace built into the TikTok app, and Shopify is a platform for running your own online store. That difference sits under every point in this comparison.
On TikTok Shop, you list products in TikTok's Seller Center. Shoppers find them in videos, LIVE streams, the Shop tab and search, and pay inside TikTok, which sets the rules on listings, checkout, shipping, returns and customer contact. It is only available in some countries, so check that your market is supported.
On Shopify, you pay for the software and build a store on your own domain. You choose the theme, the checkout settings, the apps and the payment options, and you decide how to talk to customers after they buy. Shopify does not send you shoppers. Traffic comes from your ads, search, email, social and word of mouth.

        
        
        
      
        
## Checkout: in the app vs on your own store

        TikTok Shop checkout happens inside TikTok, while Shopify checkout happens on your store. That is the biggest practical difference for conversion.
A TikTok shopper can watch a video, tap the product and pay without opening a browser. Saved payment and address details make it fast, which suits impulse purchases at lower price points. The downside is that you cannot customize the checkout, add your own upsells in the same way or show your full brand story at the moment of purchase.
A Shopify checkout sends the shopper from the ad or post to your site. That extra step loses some people, especially on mobile and in-app browsers. In return, you control the product page, bundles, post-purchase offers and subscription options, and you can test and improve every step. Brands with higher prices, longer consideration or a strong bundle and subscription model usually do better with that control.

        
        
        
      
        
## Where the traffic comes from

        TikTok Shop can bring you shoppers through TikTok's own feed, search and creators, while a Shopify store gets only the traffic you send it. That is TikTok Shop's main advantage.
On TikTok Shop, a product can get sales from organic videos, from affiliate creators who post about it and from the Shop tab and search inside the app. Paid campaigns, including [GMV Max](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/tiktok-gmv-max) and [Spark Ads](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tiktok-ads-agency), can add more. None of that is guaranteed, and organic reach rises and falls with the algorithm, but the potential audience is already in the app and already shopping.
On Shopify, every visitor has a cost or an effort behind it: Meta ads, TikTok ads, Google, SEO, email, influencers. The upside is that traffic you build, such as an email list or search rankings, keeps working regardless of one platform's policy changes. A brand that relies only on TikTok Shop is exposed if the algorithm, the fee structure or the rules change.

        
        
        
      
        
## TikTok Shop fees vs Shopify fees

        TikTok Shop mainly charges a referral fee on each sale, a percentage of the order that varies by category and region, while Shopify mainly charges a monthly plan fee plus payment processing. Both change over time, so check TikTok's current seller fee page for your market and Shopify's pricing page before you model margins. We do not quote exact rates here because they differ by country, category and date.
The bigger cost difference is usually not the platform fee itself. On TikTok Shop, creator commission and seller-funded promotions often cost more per order than the referral fee. On Shopify, paying for traffic usually costs more than the subscription and processing combined.

        
        Cost typeTikTok ShopShopifyPlatform fee per saleReferral fee as a percentage of the order, by category and region. Check TikTok's seller fee page.No sales commission when you use Shopify Payments. An extra transaction fee applies if you use a third-party payment provider.SubscriptionCheck your region's seller terms.Monthly plan fee that depends on the plan you choose.Payment processingCheck whether it is included in the referral fee or charged separately in your region.Card processing rate per order, set by your plan and region.Creator and affiliate commissionSet by you per product, paid on sales creators drive.Only if you run your own affiliate or influencer program.PromotionsSeller-funded discounts and campaign participation.Discounts you choose to run.TrafficOptional ads such as GMV Max and Spark Ads.You pay for or earn all traffic: ads, SEO, email, social.Apps and toolsSeller Center tools are included.Many brands pay monthly for apps on top of the plan.
        
### Compare margin per order, not fee rates
To compare the two fairly, work out [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin) per order on each channel. For TikTok Shop, subtract product cost, shipping, the referral fee, creator commission and any discount. For Shopify, subtract product cost, shipping, processing and the ad cost it takes to win the order. Our [break-even ROAS calculator](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator) helps with the Shopify side, and our TikTok Shop strategy guide has a worked example of TikTok Shop margin with assumed rates.

      
        
## Who owns the customer data

        On Shopify you own the customer relationship, while on TikTok Shop the buyer is TikTok's customer first. For a DTC brand that plans to grow through repeat purchases, this is often the deciding factor.
A Shopify order gives you the customer's email, and if they opt in, their phone number for SMS. You can add them to post-purchase flows, ask for reviews, offer a subscription and bring them back with a timed second-purchase offer. That repeat revenue costs very little in ads, which is where much of a DTC brand's [lifetime value](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/ltv) comes from.
A TikTok Shop order gives you what you need to ship it, but TikTok limits how you can contact or market to that buyer off the platform. Check TikTok's current seller data policy for the details in your region. You can still build a relationship inside TikTok through your account, LIVE streams and follow-up products in your shop, but you cannot simply move every buyer into your [email and SMS flows](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/klaviyo-email-sms-agency) the way you would from Shopify.

        
        
        
      
        
## Affiliates and creators

        TikTok Shop has a built-in affiliate system that makes it much easier to get creators selling your product, while Shopify needs a separate program and tooling. This is the second big reason brands add TikTok Shop.
On TikTok Shop, you set a commission rate on each product and creators can request samples, add the product to their showcase and earn on the sales they drive. Tracking, payment and attribution all happen inside TikTok. A good product with a fair commission can attract dozens or hundreds of creators without separate contracts.
On Shopify, you can run an [affiliate program](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/dtc-affiliate-program) through an app, send discount codes to influencers or pay creators for [UGC](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/viral-creatives) to use in your own ads. That works, but you handle recruitment, tracking and payment yourself, and the creator's audience still has to leave the app to buy. Our guide to building a DTC affiliate program covers that side, and many brands run both: TikTok Shop affiliates for in-app sales and paid UGC for ads that send traffic to Shopify.

        
        
        
      
        
## Fulfilment and shipping

        TikTok Shop sets strict shipping and service rules that affect your shop's standing, while Shopify lets you set your own shipping promises. You need to be ready for TikTok's rules before you turn the channel on.
On TikTok Shop, you can usually ship orders yourself or through your 3PL, and in some markets you can use Fulfilled by TikTok. Either way, TikTok tracks metrics such as late dispatch, cancellations and returns, and poor performance can lead to warnings or limits on the shop. Viral moments also create sudden spikes in orders, so stock and fulfilment capacity matter more than on a steady paid traffic channel.
On Shopify, you choose your shipping times, carriers and return policy. Customers still expect speed, and slow shipping hurts reviews and repeat purchases, but there is no platform scoring your account. If you already ship well from Shopify, the main TikTok Shop work is meeting its dispatch deadlines and keeping inventory in sync so you do not oversell.

        
        
        
      
        
## Using both: Shopify as the hub, TikTok Shop as a channel

        Most DTC brands should run Shopify as the hub for products, inventory and orders, and connect TikTok Shop to it as a sales channel. That gives you TikTok's reach without splitting your operations in two.
Shopify's TikTok app can connect your store to TikTok Shop in supported markets. Depending on your region and the current version, it can sync your product catalogue and inventory and bring TikTok Shop orders into Shopify for fulfilment. Check what the app supports in your market before you rely on it. The point is to manage stock and orders in one place, so a viral video on TikTok does not oversell items your Shopify store is also selling.
A sensible setup looks like this:

        - List a small number of hero products on TikTok Shop first, the ones that are easy to show on camera and can carry creator commission.
- Keep prices consistent across channels where you can, or have a clear reason when they differ, such as a TikTok-only bundle.
- Use TikTok Shop for discovery and impulse sales, and use Shopify for bundles, subscriptions, higher price points and repeat purchases.
- Measure each channel on contribution margin per order, not on revenue alone.
- Watch for overlap. Some TikTok Shop buyers would have bought on Shopify anyway, so check whether total sales grow or just move between channels.

        
        
      
        
## Decision guide: which should you sell on?

        Use Shopify if control, margin and repeat customers drive your business, use TikTok Shop if impulse demand and creators drive it, and use both if you have the operations to support two channels. The table below matches common situations to a starting point.

        
        Your situationStart withWhyNew brand, low-priced product that demonstrates well on videoTikTok Shop, with a basic Shopify storeTikTok brings shoppers and creators without paid traffic; Shopify gives you a home base.Established Shopify brand with steady Meta adsShopify, then add TikTok Shop as a channelKeep what works and test TikTok Shop on hero products.Higher price, longer consideration or subscription modelShopifyYou need the product page, checkout control and customer data.Brand relies on email, SMS and repeat purchasesShopify as the hubYou keep the customer contact that drives lifetime value.Thin margins that cannot carry creator commission and feesShopify, until margins improveTikTok Shop costs per order may leave nothing after the sale.Market where TikTok Shop is not availableShopifyYou can still use TikTok ads to send traffic to your store.Strong product and capacity for creators and LIVE sellingBoth, connectedShopify runs operations; TikTok Shop adds reach and creator sales.
        
### If you decide to add TikTok Shop
Start small, with a few hero products, a commission rate your margin can carry and a plan for creator samples. Our TikTok Shop strategy guide covers listings, pricing and LIVE selling in detail. If you would rather have it run for you, our TikTok Shop agency team handles setup, creators and GMV Max, and our [Shopify agency](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/shopify-agency) keeps the store converting as the hub for every channel.

      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### Should I sell on TikTok Shop or Shopify?
If you can only choose one, choose Shopify when you want control of the brand, checkout and customer data, and TikTok Shop when your product sells on impulse from short videos and you need demand. Most DTC brands do best with Shopify as the hub and TikTok Shop added as a sales channel.

### What are the TikTok Shop fees?
TikTok Shop mainly charges a referral fee on each order, a percentage that varies by product category and country, and the rates have changed over time. You also pay any creator commission you set and any discounts you fund. Check TikTok's current seller fee page for your market before modelling margins.

### Can I connect TikTok Shop to my Shopify store?
Yes, in supported markets. Shopify's TikTok app can connect your store to TikTok Shop and, depending on your region and the app version, sync products and inventory and bring TikTok Shop orders into Shopify for fulfilment. Check what it supports in your country before you launch.

### Do I get customer emails from TikTok Shop orders?
Not in the way you do on Shopify. TikTok Shop gives you the details needed to fulfil the order but limits how you can contact or market to buyers off the platform. Check TikTok's current seller data policy. If email and SMS retention matter to your business, keep Shopify as your main store.

### Is TikTok Shop cheaper than Shopify?
It depends on what you count. Shopify charges a plan fee and processing but you pay for all traffic. TikTok Shop charges a fee per order and often creator commission, but can bring shoppers without ad spend. Compare contribution margin per order on each channel, including ads, fees and commission, rather than the headline fees.

# Questions to Ask a Meta Ads Agency Before You Hire One
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/questions-to-ask-meta-ads-agency
Summary: 19 questions to ask a Meta ads agency before you hire, grouped by proof, creative, access, reporting, pricing and onboarding, with the red flags to watch for.

Direct Answer: Before you hire a Meta ads agency, ask questions in six areas: proof that they have run accounts like yours, how they make and test creative, who owns the ad account and data, what they measure and report, how they charge and what the contract locks you into, and what happens in the first 30 days. Good agencies answer with specifics and show you their work. Vague answers, guaranteed results and any plan to run ads in an account they own are red flags.

      
      
      
        
## How to use these questions

        Use these questions on a sales call with every agency on your shortlist, write down the answers, and score them the same way so you compare like with like. The goal is not to catch anyone out. It is to find out how the agency actually works before you hand over your ad account and budget.
Pay as much attention to how an agency answers as to what it says. A team that knows its process will answer quickly and with examples. A team that is selling a promise will change the subject, talk about "proprietary systems" without explaining them, or tell you what results to expect before it has seen your numbers.
Send the account ownership and pricing questions in writing before the call, so the call itself can focus on proof, creative and measurement.

        
        
        
      
        
## Proof and fit

        The first thing to find out is whether the agency has run Meta ads for brands like yours, at a similar spend, and can show it. An agency that is great at lead generation for local businesses may not know how to scale a Shopify store with a $50 product. Ask:

        - 1. Which ecommerce brands at our stage and price point have you run Meta ads for, and can we speak to one of them?
- 2. Can you walk us through a real account, with the client's permission, rather than showing screenshots of ROAS?
- 3. Who will run our account day to day, what is their experience, and how many other accounts do they manage?

        
        
### Good answer vs red flag
A good answer names relevant brands or categories, offers a reference call, and is clear about who does the work. Many agencies cannot share client accounts openly, and that is fine, but they should be able to show results in context: spend, time period, what changed and what the margin looked like.
Red flags: only screenshots of a single great day, results with no spend or time frame attached, a senior person on the sales call who disappears after signing, or a vague answer about how many accounts each media buyer looks after.

      
        
## Creative

        Ask how the agency makes and tests ads, because creative is now the main lever in most Meta accounts. Targeting is now broad and largely automated, so the ads do most of the work of finding buyers. Ask:

        - 4. Who makes the ads: your team, freelancers, creators or us? How many new concepts will you test each month?
- 5. How do you decide what to test, and how do you decide whether a test won or lost?
- 6. Who owns the creative, the raw footage and the creator usage rights when we stop working together?

        
        
### Good answer vs red flag
A good answer describes a testing rhythm, how new concepts differ from small variations of the same ad, and the metrics used to judge a test, such as cost per purchase and thumb-stop rate, over a set amount of spend. It should also be clear on who pays for creators and that you keep the files and usage rights you paid for.
Red flags: "we will use your existing ads", no answer on volume, testing judged on likes or clicks, or creative that stays with the agency when you leave. If the agency does not make creative, that can still work, but ask who will, how fast, and who writes the [creative strategy](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/creative-strategy-agency) behind the briefs.

      
        
## Account ownership and access

        Your ad account, pixel, catalogue and business portfolio should always belong to you, with the agency added as a partner. Getting this wrong can cost you your ad history and data if the relationship ends. Ask:

        - 7. Will the ad account, pixel or dataset, catalogue and Page all stay in our business portfolio?
- 8. What access level do you need, and how do we remove it if we part ways?
- 9. Whose payment method will be on the ad account, and who pays Meta directly?

        
        
### Good answer vs red flag
A good answer is simple: everything lives in your business portfolio, the agency requests partner access to the assets it needs, and your card or invoicing pays Meta directly. Removing a partner should take you a few clicks.
Red flags: running your ads from an ad account the agency owns, asking for your personal Facebook login, asking to be the only admin, or paying Meta on your behalf without a clear reason in the contract. If an agency insists on its own account, you lose the history and data when you leave, and a policy problem on its side can affect your ads too.

      
        
## Measurement and reporting

        Ask what number the agency will manage your account to, because an agency that optimizes to Meta-reported ROAS alone can look good while your bank balance does not. The target should come from your margins and be checked against your store data, not only against Ads Manager. Ask:

        - 10. What is the main number you manage to, and how will you set the target from our margins?
- 11. How do you handle the gap between what Meta reports and what Shopify shows?
- 12. Will you check our pixel and [Conversions API](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/conversions-api) setup, including event deduplication, before spending more?
- 13. What goes in a weekly report, and who walks us through it?

        
        
### Good answer vs red flag
A good answer talks about [break-even ROAS](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/tools/break-even-roas-calculator) or a target cost per acquisition built from your product cost, shipping and fees, and about checking results at a total business level, such as revenue against total ad spend, alongside platform numbers. The agency should plan to audit tracking first, because every decision after that depends on it. Reports should explain what changed, why, and what happens next.
Red flags: promising a specific ROAS before seeing your account, reporting only Meta's numbers, no interest in your margins, or reports that are a dashboard link with no commentary.

      
        
## Pricing and contract

        Ask exactly how the agency gets paid, what the fee covers and how long you are committed for, and get the answers in writing. Ask:

        - 14. How do you charge, and what exactly does the fee include?
- 15. What is the minimum term, the notice period, and what happens to our assets when it ends?
- 16. Is creative production included, or is it a separate cost? Are there setup fees?

        
        
### Good answer vs red flag
A good answer gives a clear fee structure, a written scope, and a notice period you can live with. Longer commitments are not automatically bad, since Meta accounts take time to test properly, but there should be a sensible exit if the work is not delivered.
Red flags: pricing that changes once you ask for detail, long lock-ins with no performance review points, hidden creative or "tech" fees, and guaranteed results. No agency controls Meta's auction, your product or your margins, so a guarantee usually means fine print you will not like.

      
        
## How Meta ads agency pricing models work

        Meta ads agencies usually charge in one of three ways, or a mix of them: a percentage of ad spend, a flat monthly retainer, or a performance fee. Each model rewards the agency for something different, so the right one depends on your stage and what you want the agency to focus on. The table compares them without market prices, because rates vary widely by scope, spend and what is included.

        - If you choose a performance model, agree in writing what data the fee is based on, such as Shopify revenue or [contribution margin](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/glossary/contribution-margin), and what the baseline is.
- Whatever the model, compare total cost, including creative, against the contribution margin the agency needs to add to pay for itself.
- Ask how the fee changes as you scale, so you know what you will pay at double your current spend.

        ModelHow it worksWhat it rewardsWatch out forPercentage of ad spendThe fee is a share of what you spend on Meta each month, often with a minimum fee.Managing and growing spend.The agency earns more when spend rises, whether or not that spend is profitable.Flat retainerA fixed monthly fee for an agreed scope of work.Predictable work and planning.Scope creep, and no direct link between the fee and results.Performance feePart or all of the fee is tied to an outcome, such as revenue or profit above a baseline.Hitting the agreed outcome.How the outcome is measured. Revenue-based fees can reward discounting and attributed sales that would have happened anyway.HybridA base retainer plus a performance or spend-based element.A balance of stable work and growth.Complex terms that are hard to check. Make sure you can audit the numbers.
        
### Agency, freelancer or in-house?
An agency is not always the right answer. If you spend enough to keep one person busy full time and you can manage them, an [in-house media buyer](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/compare/agency-vs-in-house-media-buyer) can work well. Our comparison of agency and in-house options covers the trade-offs, and our guide to DTC agency cost goes deeper on judging value.

      
        
## Onboarding and the first 30 days

        Ask what the agency will do in the first 30 days, because a good onboarding plan tells you more about how it works than any pitch deck. The first month should be about understanding the business, fixing tracking and setting up a testing plan, not about doubling your budget. Ask:

        - 17. What will you do in the first 30 days, week by week?
- 18. What do you need from us, such as margins, product data, past ads, access and approvals?
- 19. When, and on what numbers, should we judge whether this is working?

        
        
### Good answer vs red flag
A good answer covers an account and tracking review, a look at your margins and offers, a creative and testing plan, and a clear first round of launches. It sets a realistic review point and admits that not every early test will work.
Red flags: rebuilding the whole account on day one with no review, no questions about your margins or customers, and no agreed point at which you will judge progress. If you want an independent view before you commit, a fixed-scope [Meta ads audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/meta-ads-audit) is a lower-risk first step than a long contract.

      
        
## A simple agency scorecard

        Score each agency from 0 to 2 in each area after the call: 0 for a red flag or no answer, 1 for a reasonable but vague answer, and 2 for a specific answer backed by evidence. An agency that scores 0 on account ownership should be ruled out whatever its total, because that risk is hard to undo.

        
        AreaScores 2 when the agencyScores 0 when the agencyScore (0 to 2)Proof and fitShows relevant work in context and offers a referenceShows only screenshots or results with no contextCreativeExplains volume, testing method and ownershipHas no plan for new creativeAccount ownershipWorks as a partner in your business portfolioWants to run ads from its own accountMeasurementSets targets from your margins and audits trackingPromises a ROAS before seeing the accountPricing and contractGives a clear written scope and exit termsGuarantees results or hides feesOnboardingHas a week-by-week first month and review pointPlans to scale spend straight away
        
### Ask us the same questions
We are a [Meta ads agency](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/meta-ads-agency), so we are on the other side of these calls too. Put every one of these questions to us. If you would like a starting point before any agency conversation, our [Brand Growth Audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/book) reviews your account, tracking, creative and margins and gives you the plan whether or not you hire us.

      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### What questions should I ask a Meta ads agency?
Ask about six areas: proof that they have run accounts like yours, how they make and test creative, who owns the ad account and data, what they measure and report, how they charge and what the contract commits you to, and what they will do in the first 30 days.

### What are the red flags when hiring a Meta ads agency?
The biggest red flags are running your ads from an account the agency owns, asking for your personal Facebook login, guaranteeing a ROAS or revenue figure, reporting only Meta's numbers, hiding creative or setup fees, and long lock-ins with no review point.

### How do I choose a Meta ads agency for ecommerce?
Shortlist agencies that have run Meta ads for ecommerce brands at your stage, ask each the same questions, score the answers on proof, creative, ownership, measurement, pricing and onboarding, and speak to a reference client before you sign.

### Should the agency own my Facebook ad account?
No. The ad account, pixel or dataset, catalogue and Page should stay in your business portfolio, with the agency given partner access. That way you keep your data and history if you change agencies, and you can remove their access yourself.

### How do Meta ads agencies charge?
Most charge a percentage of ad spend, a flat monthly retainer, a performance fee tied to revenue or profit, or a hybrid of these. Rates vary widely by scope and spend, so compare total cost, including creative, against the margin the agency needs to add.

# Meta Ad Account Restricted or Disabled: What It Means and How to Get It Back
URL: https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/blog/meta-ad-account-restricted
Summary: Meta ad account restricted or disabled? Learn the four types of restriction, where to check status, how to request a review and how DTC brands prevent it.

Direct Answer: A restricted or disabled Meta ad account means Meta has stopped that account, your profile or your whole business portfolio from running ads, usually because its systems flagged a policy issue, a payment problem or suspicious activity. Check the status in Account Quality, read the reason Meta gives, fix what you can, and request a review there. Do not open new accounts to keep advertising, because Meta treats that as circumvention.

      
      Meta ad account restriction: A limit Meta places on an ad account, a person's ability to advertise, or a business portfolio when it believes Meta's Advertising Standards, Community Standards or payment terms have been broken. Restricted assets cannot run ads until the issue is resolved or a review succeeds.

      
        
## Disabled, restricted, portfolio restricted or ad rejected?

        There are four different problems that people describe as "my ad account got banned", and each one is fixed differently. Work out which one you have before you do anything else.

        - An ad rejection is the mildest. You can edit the ad or request a review of that ad on its own.
- Repeated rejections matter, though. A pattern of rejected ads can lead to wider restrictions on the account or the people running it.
- A profile restriction follows the person, not the brand. If your media buyer's profile is restricted, adding a different admin may let the brand keep advertising while that person appeals.

        What you seeWhat is affectedWhat it usually meansAd account disabledOne ad account. Its ads stop and you cannot create new ones in it.Meta flagged activity in that account, such as policy violations, a payment problem or suspicious behaviour.Advertising access restricted on a profileA person's Facebook profile. They cannot create or manage ads on any account, even ones they admin.Meta has concerns about that person's activity, identity or links to other restricted assets.Business portfolio restrictedThe whole business portfolio (formerly Business Manager) and often every ad account inside it.Meta flagged the business itself, its admins or the assets connected to it.Ad rejectedOne ad. Other ads keep running.That ad, its landing page or its targeting did not meet Meta's Advertising Standards.
        
      
        
## Where to check your status

        Check your status in Account Quality, Meta's page for the restrictions on your profile, ad accounts, Pages and business portfolio. Meta's current help pages use two names for it: some send you to Account Quality, and the ads review policy page sends you to Business Support Home. Use whichever your account shows; both list the restriction, its reason and the request review option.
You can usually reach Account Quality from Meta Business Suite, from the menu in Ads Manager, or from the notice Meta shows when an asset is restricted. It lists each restricted asset, the reason Meta gives, and whether you can request a review. Meta also sends notices by email and in the Business Suite notifications, so check those too.
Read the stated reason closely. "Unacceptable business practices", "circumventing systems", "unpaid balance" and a specific ad policy all point to different fixes. If the reason is unclear, open the Meta Business Help Center for the latest guidance on that reason, because Meta updates the wording, menus and options regularly.

        
        
        
      
        
## How to request a review

        If you believe the restriction is a mistake, or you have fixed the cause, request a review from Account Quality. Select the restricted asset, choose the option to request a review, and follow the steps Meta shows. The steps vary by restriction type and region, and Meta may ask you to confirm your identity, for example with an ID document or a short video selfie, or to secure your account first.
Before you submit, do the groundwork:

        - Fix what caused it. Edit or remove ads that break policy, clean up landing pages and settle any unpaid balance.
- Secure every profile involved. Turn on two-factor authentication and remove any admins or partners you do not recognise.
- Keep your explanation short and factual if Meta gives you a space to write one. Explain what the business sells and what you changed.
- Request one review per asset and wait. The number of reviews you can request may be limited, and some decisions are final.
- Keep a record of dates, screenshots and the reasons shown, in case you need to contact Meta support or your rep later.

        
        
### How long does a review take?
Meta does not commit to a fixed review time, and it varies by case. Some reviews come back quickly and others take much longer. Account Quality shows when a review is in progress and the outcome when it is done. If you have a Meta marketing rep through an agency or your own spend, they may be able to help you find the right support route, but they cannot overrule a policy decision.

      
        
## Common causes for DTC brands

        Most restrictions on DTC brands come from ad copy and claims, payment problems, unusual account behaviour or a poor buyer experience. Meta's systems are largely automated, so it is the pattern of signals that matters, not intent. These are the causes we see most often.

        - Health and before-and-after claims. Supplements, skincare and weight management ads that promise outcomes or show dramatic before-and-after images often break Meta's policies on health and personal health claims.
- Personal attributes wording. Meta does not allow ads that assert or imply someone's personal attributes, such as a health condition or financial situation. "Struggling with acne?" or "Tired of your belly fat?" can be enough.
- Payment failures. A declined card or an unpaid balance can disable an ad account until the balance is settled.
- Sudden spend spikes on new accounts. A brand-new ad account that jumps straight to a large daily budget can look like a compromised or fraudulent account.
- Circumvention signals. Links to previously disabled accounts or profiles, landing pages that show reviewers something different from users, or using someone else's account to keep advertising.
- Low customer feedback. Meta collects feedback from people who bought after seeing your ads. A low feedback score, often from slow shipping or products that do not match the ad, can reduce delivery and in some cases lead to restrictions.
- Compromised accounts. A hacked admin profile that runs unfamiliar ads, often in another currency or market, can get the whole portfolio restricted.

        
        
### Higher-risk categories
Supplements, health and wellness, skincare, weight management and anything that touches medical claims draw the most scrutiny. If you sell in these categories, write ads that describe the product and the experience of using it rather than promising a result, and make sure the landing page follows the same rules. Our health and wellness and supplement pages cover how we approach compliant creative for these brands.

      
        
## Payment failures and unpaid balances

        A payment restriction is usually the quickest to fix: pay the outstanding balance and the account can often return to normal. Go to Billing and payments for the ad account, check the failed charge, and either retry it or add a working payment method and pay the balance.
To stop it happening again, keep a backup payment method on the account, make sure your card limit can cover your daily spend, and tell your bank to expect regular charges from Meta. Give each ad account its own payment method where you can, so one failed card does not affect every account in the portfolio. If the account stays disabled after the balance is paid, request a review from Account Quality.

        
        
        
      
        
## What not to do

        Do not open new ad accounts, profiles or business portfolios to keep advertising while you are restricted. Meta treats this as circumvention, and it is one of the surest ways to turn a fixable restriction into a permanent one across every asset you own.
Avoid these as well:

        - Buying, renting or borrowing ad accounts or profiles from other people.
- Paying "unban" services that ask for your login details. They often cannot do what they promise, and sharing logins puts your assets at further risk.
- Resubmitting the same rejected ad again and again without changing it.
- Using landing pages or redirects that show Meta's reviewers something different from what customers see.
- Deleting the assets or admins involved and starting over. Meta can link new assets to old ones.

        
        
      
        
## Prevention checklist

        The best defence against a restricted Meta ad account is a well-set-up business portfolio, a gradual spend ramp and ads and pages that follow policy from the start. Work through this list once, then review it whenever you add a new ad account or team member. A [Meta ads audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/meta-ads-audit) should include the same checks.

        - Verify your business in the business portfolio settings, using your registered business details.
- Turn on two-factor authentication for every person with access, and require it in the portfolio settings.
- Have at least two trusted admins, so one restricted or locked-out profile does not lock the brand out.
- Give agencies and freelancers partner access through their own business portfolio rather than sharing logins.
- Ramp spend gradually on new ad accounts instead of starting at full budget.
- Keep landing pages compliant: clear business details, contact information, shipping and returns policies, and claims that match the ads.
- Use separate payment methods for each ad account, plus a backup card.
- Check your ads against Meta's Advertising Standards before launch, especially health, personal attributes and before-and-after content.
- Watch your customer feedback score and fix shipping or product issues that drive complaints.
- Check Account Quality every week, so you catch warnings and rejected ads before they build up.

        
        
### If you are restricted right now
Confirm which of the four problems you have, read the reason in Account Quality, fix the cause, secure your accounts and request a review. Check the Meta Business Help Center for the current steps, since the process changes. Then use the waiting time to fix the setup issues on this list, so the next account you run is harder to restrict. If you want a second pair of eyes on the setup, our team can review it as part of a [Brand Growth Audit](https://www.brandscalinghacks.com/book).

      
      
## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why was my Meta ad account restricted?
Meta restricts ad accounts when its systems flag policy violations, payment problems or suspicious activity. For DTC brands the common causes are health or before-and-after claims, personal attributes wording, failed payments, sudden spend spikes on new accounts and signs of circumvention. Account Quality shows the reason Meta gives.

### How do I get my Facebook ad account back?
Open Account Quality, find the disabled account, read the reason, fix the cause and request a review. Meta may ask you to verify your identity or secure your account first. If the cause is an unpaid balance, paying it often restores the account.

### What is the difference between a disabled ad account and restricted advertising access?
A disabled ad account affects one ad account. Restricted advertising access affects a person's profile, so they cannot run or manage ads on any account. A business portfolio restriction can affect every ad account inside the portfolio.

### How long does a Meta ad account review take?
Meta does not publish a fixed time, and it varies by case. Account Quality shows when a review is in progress and the outcome when it is complete. Check the Meta Business Help Center for current guidance.

### Can I just create a new ad account if mine is disabled?
No. Opening new ad accounts, profiles or business portfolios to keep advertising while restricted is treated by Meta as circumventing its systems, and it can lead to permanent restrictions on everything linked to you. Request a review instead.

- Troubleshoot a disabled ad account (Meta Business Help Center)

- Ads review policy (Meta for Business)
